items.text:
Spanish economist de Cos to succeed Lagarde as head of ECB
Spanish monetary economist Pablo Hernandez de Cos on Thursday was set to replace France's Christine Lagarde as the new head of the European Central Bank (ECB). His nomination comes as the Europe's most powerful financial institution grapples with an Iran war-driven resurgence in inflation and a cost of living crisis.
European leaders on Thursday chose the former head of Spain’s central bank, Pablo Hernandez de Cos, to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank (ECB) as the key EU institution confronts inflation driven by the war in Iran and worries about high government debt and borrowing costs in Europe.
Leaders from the 21 European member countries that use the euro also filled two other top posts at the ECB, which decides borrowing costs for the 359 million people in the eurozone.
Agreement on the three posts was reached at a summit in Brussels, said an EU diplomat tasked with communicating for the Irish Presidency and speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to be named. French President Emmanuel Macron confirmed the result on X.
De Cos' nomination still must pass review by the European Parliament and the ECB’s governing council, but those steps are formalities.
The former Spanish central bank governor and the current general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, will take over when current chief Lagarde steps down ‌early on February 7.
Read moreECB President Christine Lagarde to step down in February 2027, nine months before term ends
The way for him to replace her as the next ECB chief became clear on Thursday after the Netherlands decided to back him, effectively standing down its own candidate Klaas Knot.
The reshuffle comes as the ECB grapples with an Iran war-driven resurgence in inflation and worries that political turmoil in France could trigger broader financial market stress affecting other euro zone countries.
De Cos' appointment hands the top job to a southern European policymaker and ally ‌of former ECB President Mario Draghi, reinforcing expectations that the central bank would ultimately use its firepower to contain any new sovereign debt crisis.
His formal approval will come from a meeting of ambassadors of Eurozone countries on Thursday, ahead of endorsement from the bloc’s leaders.
Steady hand
De Cos, 55, a trained monetary economist, has built a reputation for independent thinking anchored in economic theory, and pragmatism picked up over a decade served in policymaking roles.
He worked in various staff positions at the ECB and the Bank of Spain early in his career before making a rare jump to the policymaking level as governor of the national central bank, serving on the ECB's rate-setting Governing Council.
De Cos is a veteran of crises including Spain's banking sector bailout, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the post-pandemic inflation surge that forced the ECB into its fastest interest rate-hiking cycle on record.
While southern European policymakers are often considered "doves" favouring easier monetary policy, colleagues and ECB watchers say De Cos is pragmatic and a moderate who cannot be boxed into any such category.
ECB policy is decided by the 27-member Governing Council, meaning even the president has limited scope to steer interest rates single-handedly.
In any case, any dovish bias would only be relevant if inflation was slightly above target, and this year's surge in price pressures would force any ECB president to keep raising interest rates.
At 4 percent, inflation is now twice the central bank's target and policymakers speaking on and off the record appear unanimous that a rate hike in December is inevitable.
The path beyond is murky, however. Markets expect just one more upward move, given the recent retreat in oil prices and an expected decline in inflation from the spring, when statistical base effects start knocking year-earlier figures from the data set.
(FRANCE 24 with AP and Reuters)

George Russell says he was "amused" by Max Verstappen’s criticism of him after their feud reignited at the Las Vegas Grand Prix but admits it was "avoidable".
After colliding on track in final practice last weekend, Russell publicly criticised Verstappen following the incident. The Dutchman won the race after an intense battle between them and said afterwards that the Mercedes driver is "far below my level".
The pair have clashed several times on track in the past, most notably engaging in a remarkable war of words following an incident during qualifying at the 2024 Qatar Grand Prix where Verstappen felt Russell had pushed unreasonably hard for him to be penalised.

Speaking on Thursday - back at the Lusail International Circuit almost exactly two years on from that incident - ahead of this weekend's Qatar Grand Prix, Russell said: "At the end of the day, I guess I stand by what I said after practice.
"But he was the one who went out and won the race. I didn't and I'm sure he had a bit of a laugh about that, and that was reasonably amusing. From my side, just a new race weekend, try and focus on the driving and move on."
Russell was pressed on the saga throughout the FIA press conference and revealed he was perhaps "guilty of being just too open and honest when I speak with you guys [the media]".
"It's all avoidable at the end of the day, and it's all a bit unnecessary. It's not something I'm looking to continue. I'm not looking to have poor relationships with people. That's just not really the type of person I am," he said.
"There are lessons just to be taken away from these situations. Maybe I am just too open and honest with the media because I feel that I'm having more of an open conversation with you guys as opposed to remembering there's a camera.
"There are more people in this room than there are cameras, and I feel like I'm talking to you, but I'm not actually talking to you. I need to remind myself that I'm talking to the camera there that's broadcasting to millions of people. That's the biggest takeaway."

After Chelsea fell to back-to-back losses with a 4-1 humiliation by Leeds at Stamford Bridge last Saturday, Sky Sports News reporter James Savundra examines the latest developments at Stamford Bridge.
As well as suffering a third defeat in four Premier League games, Chelsea and manager Xabi Alonso also faced the added frustration of defender Wesley Fofana giving an unauthorised interview this week, in which he laughed off his penalty miss in last month's Carabao Cup defeat to Liverpool and revealed he had contemplated retiring during his time at Stamford Bridge.

Will Fofana face disciplinary action?
Jake: Is Fofana expected to face any disciplinary action for his impromptu interview? Some of the things said in that were unacceptable from a footballer, especially one involved in as much off-the-pitch controversy as him.
James says: Xabi Alonso addressed this at Thursday's press conference. Fofana has apologised following the interview. The matter has been dealt with internally and there are no suggestions that the defender is set to miss any matches.
Whether the club look to punish Fofana with a fine is not known at this stage. Alonso made clear that this will not be repeated. It's completely understandable to emphasise with Chelsea supporters. Fofana simply hasn't justified the £75m that Chelsea paid Leicester City.
Why is he still in the team?
Benny: Why is Fofana still being chosen when every single fan watching football can see how poor his form is?
James says: At the moment there is a lack of real alternative options. Xabi Alonso stood behind the Fofana-Colwill axis during Thursday's press conference despite their clear struggles dealing with Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Brian Brobbey.
Liam Delap will prove a similar physical threat tomorrow [Friday] with an added point to prove. Ultimately, Chelsea trimmed down their squad in the summer in light of no European football. Maxence Lacroix would be starting, possibly ahead of Fofana right now if he was fit.
Colwill has found things difficult this season having missed the majority of the last campaign. In hindsight, should Chelsea have sold Trevoh Chalobah? Perhaps it was time for the academy graduate to end his Chelsea chapter but he rarely let the side down.
You could feasibly play Josh Acheampong at centre-back. The youngster has been a shining light this season. Yet he looks comfortable on the right. Do you want to upset something which actually seems to be working. And if Acheampong moves to centre-back, then does Marco Palestra play as a right-back?
The Italian impressed in Serie A as a wing-back but with Chelsea opting largely for a flat back four, is Palestra defensively good enough to fulfil that role. Aaron Anselmino remains an option but hasn't played a minute for the club this season.
Will Chelsea invest in January?
Mikey: Will Chelsea sell and buy any defenders and strikers in January? I feel we need stronger defenders with a better aerial ability and maybe a more out and out No 9 to challenge Joao Pedro and give us something different.
James says: Chelsea will spend money in January if they believe it will help them achieve their target this season - qualifying for the Champions League. They were pleased with what they did in the summer but accept that the squad still requires investment.
It seems unlikely any defenders will be sold given the lack of current options. A loan move would seem to suit Aaron Anselmino given his lack of options. The winter window is a difficult one. There's a sense that Chelsea could benefit from signing a more experienced centre-back, considering the moves for Emi Martinez, Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck in every other area of the pitch in the summer.
The club have shown a willingness to tweak their transfer model and sign players for the here and now, in addition to targeting players for the future. A striker would appear unlikely given the presence of Emmanuel Emegha and Danny Welbeck. It will be interesting to watch Emegha's development if given a run of games in the absence of Joao Pedro.

Playing Rogers or Pedro Neto as a false-nine has been experimented with but Chelsea have looked blunt without a focal point - though Emmanuel Emegha scored in his first Premier League start which was really encouraging.

items.text:
A LILLE SPOT OF BOTHER
Bayern Munich’s 2-1 defeat to Lille was arguably the most eye-catching of Wednesday night’s Bigger Cup results, but anyone who tuned into proceedings at Stade Pierre-Mauroy will have been unsurprised by the outcome. Not so much an elite European tie as a game of Name That Bayern Reserve, the German champions’ starting lineup resembled a pale facsimile of its usual self. Their current knack-list includes such high-profile names as – deep breath – Harry Kane, Michael Olise, Alphonso Davies, Manuel Neuer, Serge Gnabry, Luis Díaz, Jamal Musiala and Ismael Saibari. And with Díaz and Musiala only fit enough for places on the bench, Konrad Laimer was deployed as a makeshift striker. The veteran right-back is famously as handy as a small pot, but filling Kane’s iconic Skechers proved a task too far for the Austrian.
Lille’s winner came from a similarly unlikely source of goals for the French side, with Aleksandar Pavlovic popping up to score a hilarious own goal that left his Bayern teammates giving him the collective stink-eye as he sank to his knees, head in hands in the traditional mea culpa style. Having seen Ethan Mbappé played clean through courtesy of a lightning-fast Lille counterattack, Pavlovic sprinted back towards his own team’s goal like a cheating spouse who’s just realised they left their phone unlocked on the coffee table. Although his panicked chase looked to be in vain, the German hit pay-dirt when Mbappé rolled his low shot past Bayern goalkeeper Jonas Urbig, only to see it rebound off the foot of the post. Cue Pavlovic, who accidentally stabbed the ball into the gaping goal as he attempted what appeared to be the routine task of putting it out for a corner.
While Pavlovic’s own goal was definitely the funniest Bayern have scored in recent memory, it certainly wasn’t the most embarrassing. That dubious honour goes to assorted club blazers including Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, Uli Hoeness and Jan-Christian Dreesen, who have publicly questioned whether Musiala is worth the astronomical wages he is paid, given his struggles with knack and recent diagnosis with a treatable neurological disorder. Rummenigge even went so far as to suggest that if the 23-year-old does not return to top form, the remaining four years of his contract would “no longer be justifiable” and suggested a pay cut might be in order. Asked about this tone-deaf and decidedly mercenary invasion of his teammate’s medical privacy by club officials, Joshua Kimmich gave his superiors both barrels. “What I don’t understand is the way this is being communicated in public,” he harrumphed. “It must never happen that the burden is placed on a player. The club is obviously the top priority and bigger than a player, but it’s not bigger than a person. That’s an absolute no-go and it is not Bayern-like.” Neither is the shame of being second in the Bundesliga while languishing in 15th place in Bigger Cup Monster Group, but don’t expect anyone in the club boardroom to volunteer to trim their wages accordingly.
LIVE ON BIG WEBSITE
Join Will Unwin from 8pm for hot Big Vase action, including Sunderland 2-1 Jagiellonia, Torreense 1-1 Celtic and Crystal Palace 1-1 Real Sociedad, plus reaction from Celta Vigo 0-1 Bournemouth, Brighton 3-0 Universitatea Craoiva and Hearts 0-3 Monaco.
QUOTE OF THE DAY
“Stability in a company is having standards. Everybody who joins commits to the standards. I think, very honestly, the standards were not high enough. We have players who are here for four years, [who] can’t speak English. If you go to Italy, after three months, every player gives his interview in the Italian language. For me, if I want to manage in England, I have to speak English” – Oliver Glasner puts his Nottingham Forest squad’s linguistic skills on blast.
FOOTBALL DAILY LETTERS
 
 I liked Erling Haaland’s observation that football can simultaneously be “easy and difficult” [yesterday’s Football Daily]. That got me thinking about other things that have conflicting characteristics. Soup can be both sweet and sour. My feelings for my partner often run hot and cold. And my daily tea-timely newsletter can be mildly funny and mildly unfunny – Mike Wilner.
 
 The constant change in Watford manager, a once fine club whose first two managers lasted a total of 23 years, is now so high that I don’t even notice it anymore ... apparently this was yesterday, and I’ve no idea who the previous bloke was. Watford are now onto their 30th manager, including caretakers, although in practice they’re all just caretaker managers, since the Pozzos took over in 2012. I don’t know whether to laugh at, or cry for, the Watford fans (Narrator: it’s the former, obviously) – Noble Francis.
If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Mike Wilner. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

items.text:
Qatari, Egyptian leaders discuss Gaza ‘ceasefire’ and regional security
Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani is in Cairo for an official visit aimed at further strengthening bilateral relations.
Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi have discussed regional tensions and efforts to implement the Gaza “ceasefire” during talks in Cairo.
El-Sisi received the emir on Thursday at Cairo International Airport upon his arrival for an official visit at the Egyptian president’s invitation. After a reception at the presidential palace, the talks began.
Sheikh Tamim’s visit was aimed at further strengthening bilateral relations across various sectors, including investment and energy, as well as coordinating diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions and bolster regional security, Qatar said.
“Today, I discussed with my brother, President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, the latest developments in the region and the importance of continuing consultations and coordinating joint efforts to address current challenges, in a way that helps safeguard our region’s security and stability and fulfil its peoples’ aspirations for peace and prosperity,” Sheikh Tamim said on X after the meeting.
The two leaders discussed efforts to promote regional stability, Egyptian presidential spokesman Mohamed el-Shenawy said in a statement.
They stressed the importance of “intensifying regional and international efforts to prioritise political solutions and dialogue and prevent tensions from widening”, warning of “serious consequences for regional and international security and stability”, the statement added.
The talks also addressed developments in Palestine with el-Sisi outlining Egypt’s efforts to implement the Gaza “ceasefire”.
The Egyptian leader emphasised the need for all parties to uphold the agreement, ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid to the Gaza Strip and begin recovery and reconstruction programmes without delay.
Qatar’s Emiri Diwan said in a statement that the two leaders exchanged views on the latest regional and international developments, “particularly the situation in the Gaza Strip and joint mediation efforts to solidify the ceasefire”.
The Egyptian statement said el-Sisi also reaffirmed Egypt’s “full support for the security of Qatar and other Gulf states”, stressing that “the security of the Gulf is an integral part of Egypt’s national security”.
It also said the two leaders discussed ways to strengthen economic ties and cooperation in areas of mutual interest and they agreed to continue “intensifying political consultations and coordination”.
The meeting was also attended by Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani and other senior officials from both countries.

items.text:
How far-right Vox is winning over young voters ahead of Spain's snap election
Spain's Vox party is winning over many young people ahead of the country's snap election on November 29, particularly men. The far-right party is capitalising on the rising cost of living and anti-immigrant sentiment to expand its once-marginal electoral base.
In Spain, a growing number of young people say they will support the far-right, anti-immigrant Vox party in this Sunday's key snap election, according to recent polling.
One of those voters is Andres, a 19-year-old student in Madrid who told the news outlet Infobae that he believed Santiago Abascal, Vox's leader, “is undoubtedly the most logical choice” in the parliamentary election.
Andres is Catholic, believes that life starts at conception, opposes what he calls “LGBT+ ideology” and says he supports the idea of a traditional family.
Read moreSpain's right holds poll lead over Sanchez's Socialists ahead of November 29 snap election
He is among around 23.2 percent of people between the ages of 18 and 24 in Spain who support Vox, according to the latest data from the Spanish Centre for Sociological Research published in November.
That is just above the 22 percent who support Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s Partido Socialista Obrero Espanol (PSOE), commonly known in English as just the Socialists.
That is a huge jump from 2023, when only 15.4 percent of people from the same age group voted for Abascal’s party. The same increase has been noted among people between 25 and 34 years old, with polls suggesting that support for Vox has jumped from 15 percent during the last election to 22 percent in 2026.
This marks a turning point for Spain, as for the first time since the end of Francisco Franco’s fascist government in 1975, the far right could join the country’s government.
Watch moreSpain’s political crossroads, Europe’s wider stakes: Spaniards to vote in key election
The centre-right People’s Party, currently leading in the polls at 31.5 percent, has not ruled out an alliance with Vox.
One reason for this rise in support is because “this is a generation of young people facing significant economic challenges who have never experienced the dictatorship”, explained Maria Elisa Alonso, a political scientist and lecturer-researcher at the Université de Lorraine specialising in Spain.
And because of this, they are drawn to the "narrative that blames immigrants for all the country's problems".
Economic insecurity
Young people in Spain are struggling to become independent. On average, they move out of their parents’ home at about the age of 30, while their counterparts in the rest of the European Union do so at around 26, according to Eurostat.
One key factor behind this divide is soaring rent costs and hurdles to homeownership.
An average renter could pay around €1,170 to rent a 50-square-metre apartment in Madrid, according to the real estate portal Idealista. That is nearly half the average gross salary of €2,460, according to Spain's National Institute of Statistics.
Vox has promised to deregulate land use, lower taxes and combat illegal squatting to tackle the problem. But above all else, Abascal’s party has blamed the left and immigrants for the high cost of living.
Immigration has become a key topic on the campaign trail ahead of the general election, spurred by the arrival of more than 70,000 migrants from Morocco in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, in North Africa, in late July. The vast majority of those migrants have since returned home.
Immigration is a regular topic at Vox rallies. At one event, the party's leader Abascal denounced people he claimed lived “off the social benefits that Spaniards need and who have no business being in Spain”. He added that “rapists” and “murderers” should be held “in prisons in their own countries”. And he called for a “remigration” policy to, in his words, “reverse the migrant invasion”.
“Vox’s message is very simple," Alonso said. "There isn’t really a political platform. Everything is the fault of immigration. They conflate immigration with crime."
“It’s a narrative that resonates with these disillusioned young people.”
Social media and masculinism
Vox uses social media to attract young voters, regularly posting short videos on patriotism, national identity, the traditional family and anti-feminist ideology on TikTok, Instagram and X.

A media outlet close to Vox has also been accused of spreading misinformation on social media. According to FRANCE 24’s Observers team, social media users accused immigrants of election fraud after the outlet published an article alleging fraudulent registrations in a town near Madrid.
“There is a lack of critical thinking among some Spanish youth, a difficulty in discerning what is true, what is false, and what amounts to manipulation,” Alonso warned.
There is also a gender divide among Vox supporters. While support for the far-right party has generally increased among young people, men in this group are more likely than women to support Vox.
Around a quarter of male voters under 35 intend to vote for the party, according to a survey by the 40dB institute published by Cadena SER radio.
Only an estimated 20 percent among women of the same age said that they supported Vox.
By contrast, around 32 percent of young women supported Sanchez’s PSOE.
This trend is not unique to Spain, as female voters are more likely than their male counterparts to support progressive views in Europe and in the United States.

items.text:
Two Italians killed after Iranian strike in Kuwait
- Published
Two Italian nationals have died after an Iranian strike on a facility in Kuwait, Italy's foreign ministry has said.
The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, the ministry added.
Kuwait's defence ministry earlier said that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.
It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.
Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.
The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.
Meanwhile, Italy's foreign ministry said in a statement: "An explosion caused by a drone attack... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working."
The two Italian nationals were working at an air defence detection station and performing maintenance work on systems used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa, citing Italy's foreign ministry.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."

The judge said the FCC chair has taken US President Donald Trump’s rhetoric ‌‌as his ‘marching orders’.
A United States judge has barred the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from putting the licences of eight Walt Disney-owne
items.text:
US judge blocks Trump’s FCC attempt to target Disney’s ABC stations
The judge said the FCC chair has taken US President Donald Trump’s rhetoric ‌‌as his ‘marching orders’.
A United States judge has barred the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from putting the licences of eight Walt Disney-owned ABC TV stations up for early review, a blow to President Donald Trump’s efforts to rein in US media companies.
US District Judge Loren AliKhan, in Washington, DC, granted Disney’s request for a preliminary injunction on Wednesday. The injunction barred the FCC from holding a hearing on the licences, a step that could have led to their revocation and forced the stations off the air.
“This is not a close case,” AliKhan wrote, saying the FCC appeared to be carrying out a retaliatory campaign, driven by Trump, that threatened the broadcaster’s free-speech rights.
AliKhan, who was nominated by former President Joe Biden, said ABC had detailed “a campaign of retaliation against them in response to their exercise of their First Amendment rights,” which on its own is an ‘irreparable injury’”.
FCC Chair Brendan Carr, whom Trump named to the position in January 2025, “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders”, the judge added.
A spokesperson for ABC News said, “Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment.”
Carr ordered reviews of licences ‌for the eight stations in April, a day after Trump urged ABC to fire late-night host Jimmy Kimmel, even though the renewals were not due to be considered until October 2028 at the earliest. The FCC had not ordered an early review in more than 50 years before April.
Disney and ABC sued the FCC in August to block the early review of the stations in Los Angeles, Chicago, New York and other cities, arguing that the Trump administration was trying to punish the network over broadcast content in violation of the US Constitution.
In response to AliKhan’s decision, an FCC spokesperson has said that the granting of the injunction was “wrong on the facts and wrong on the law — as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear.”
They added, “We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.”
Trump has repeatedly urged broadcasters to drop comedy or news programmes that he dislikes or that have been critical of him or his administration.
Broadcast stations need FCC licences to use public airwaves. While licence revocations are extremely rare, critics said that the risk of losing a licence could have a chilling effect on a broadcaster and raise concerns about government interference.
Trump has waged aggressive attacks on the news media, and the latest move follows a two-year-long battle between Trump and Disney.
In July, Trump repeated a call for ABC stations to lose their licences because the network refused to air a prime-time speech he gave that said US elections are vulnerable to fraud.
In reacting to the judicial decision, Democratic FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez said the ruling “brings ‌‌badly needed accountability to a commission and an administration that have politicised the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control”.
The FCC is also investigating ABC daytime talk show “The View,” which discusses US politics, after saying it may be subject to federal rules requiring broadcasters ‌‌to ‌‌provide equal-time opportunities to political candidates.
Disney previously said that as a result of that investigation, the programme did not invite any political candidates to appear before the November midterm elections, and the broadcaster cited the FCC’s “pressure campaign”.

items.text:
Is authoritarian Vietnam ready to phase out the death penalty?
November 26, 2026
Vietnam, a country once considered one of the world's most prolific executioners, is steadily reducing the number of crimes punishable by death.
On November 20, the country's National Assembly approved a revised Penal Code that abolishes capital punishment for six offenses, including drug trafficking, rape of a person under the age of 16 and crimes against humanity.
When the legislation takes effect next March, just four offences — treason, murder, terrorism and illegal drug production — will remain punishable by death, down from 44 in 1997.
Although Hanoi has given little indication that it intends to do away with capital punishment entirely, few countries that still regularly execute prisoners have narrowed its legal application so considerably.
Authoritarian Vietnam's crime reforms
The reforms are particularly striking given that they come as Vietnam's ruling Communist Party has intensified its crackdown on political dissent and independent civil society.
Minister of Public Security General Luong Tam Quang said the changes reflect humanitarian considerations, the need for more proportionate sentencing and Vietnam's international integration, while maintaining a tough approach to crime, according to the state-run Vietnam News Agency.
Vietnam's gradual reduction in the number of offenses punishable by death reflects an evolution in its criminal justice philosophy, said Tran Dai Lam, a lawyer at the ANVI law firm in Hanoi.
"There is a growing recognition that the effectiveness of criminal law depends not necessarily on the severity of punishment, but on the certainty that criminal offenses are detected, prosecuted and punished," he told DW.
Moving towards abolishing the death penalty?
Vietnam's latest reforms come barely a year after the National Assembly abolished the death penalty for eight other offenses, including embezzlement, bribery, espionage and the illegal transportation of drugs.
The removal of capital punishment for drug trafficking is particularly significant given the prominence of narcotics-related offenses in Vietnam's criminal justice system and the country's proximity to the Golden Triangle, one of the world's largest illicit drug-producing regions.
The new legislation also provides for existing death sentences to be commuted to life imprisonment for offenses that will no longer carry the death penalty.
Hai Luong, a lecturer in criminology at Griffith University in Australia, told DW that Vietnam has been taking a "retentionist-but-reductionist" approach.
"Vietnam is reforming the death penalty rather than abolishing it," he said. "The trend is towards a more limited and selective use of capital punishment, but not yet towards its complete removal."
According to Luong, the gradual reduction in capital offenses reflects Hanoi's efforts to modernize its legal system without relinquishing its authority to severely punish what it considers the most serious crimes.
Vietnam's integration into international norms
Growing international recognition that capital punishment has little additional deterrent effect is also informing Vietnam's approach, he explained.
Decades of harsh penalties for drug-related offenses have done little to stem the international narcotics trade, while the continued expansion of drug trafficking networks in Southeast Asia has raised questions about the effectiveness of executions as a crime prevention measure.
Vietnam's growing integration into the international community, including its participation in international drug control conventions and closer diplomatic ties with Western countries, has also given Hanoi greater incentives to align its criminal justice system with international standards, Luong added.
Vietnam's gradual retreat from capital punishment could also bring it closer to the European Union on human rights.
Brussels has repeatedly called on Hanoi to abolish capital punishment, a subject regularly raised during bilateral human rights discussions.
The EU, one of the world's most vocal advocates of abolition, has long opposed capital punishment as part of its foreign policy.
An EU spokesperson told DW that Brussels welcomes "Vietnam's latest reduction in crimes punishable by capital punishment. This is a positive step and shows a disposition to consider gradual reform, leading towards a moratorium first and finally to the abolition of the death penalty."
"Any concrete step towards this ultimate goal would be very much welcomed by the EU," they added.
However, Vietnam's reforms still fall short of international human rights standards, particularly since the death penalty remains available for drug-related offenses that do not involve intentional killing.
Nor is there much evidence that progress on capital punishment is accompanied by improvements in other areas of Vietnam's human rights record, notably freedom of expression and association.
How often is the death penalty used in Vietnam?
It is also difficult to establish whether Vietnam's legislative reforms have resulted in fewer executions.
The authorities classify execution statistics as state secrets. Amnesty International believes Vietnam continues to make extensive use of capital punishment, but it cannot provide reliable annual figures.
Vietnam's capital punishment reform allows the state to continue executing people to fulfil its political and public security goals, "while also managing, or massaging, its international reputation through highly publicized 'reductionist' reforms," Daniel Pascoe, an associate professor of law at the City University of Hong Kong and an expert on capital punishment, told DW
For example, he added, although the recent abolition of the death penalty for drug trafficking is welcome, "it doesn't tell us whether the Vietnamese authorities will now simply charge a higher number of suspects with the drug production offense, which remains death-eligible."

items.text:
Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
- Published
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.
The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
Regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had been originally reported. The vessel remains, however, partially submerged.
That made conditions more favourable for carrying out recovery operations, he said, "as we have gone from the possibility of the vessel being at a depth of 1,000m to a situation that allows operations to be carried out on the surface".
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.
Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline. It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

items.text:
Andalusia offers a glimpse of Spain’s future as the far right gains ground
Ahead of Sunday’s election, Andalusia signals Vox’s rise as immigration and right-wing alliances reshape Spain’s politics.
Andalusia, Spain – Surrounded by shelves heaving with canned goods and cured meats, the owners of a family-run grocery store are locked in a debate about Spain’s upcoming elections.
All politicians are “liars”, proclaims 32-year-old Antonio Cerezo, announcing he will cast a blank ballot. His cousin, Patricia Nicolas Cerezo, 43, is less certain, riddled with doubt about who to support.
As for her 18-year-old son, first-time voter Alfonso Duque, the only choice is the far-right Vox party: “It can’t get worse than this”.
The one thing that the family in the small village of Rioja seems to agree on is that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s socialists must go.
A former socialist bastion, the southern region’s political landscape has changed. Since May’s regional election, it has been governed by a coalition of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox, once a fringe party that has drawn support by championing migrant deportations and tapping into a wider wave of far-right, anti-establishment support across Europe.
Ahead of Sunday’s snap vote, observers say Andalusia’s political dynamics could offer a glimpse of what might come next nationally.
That arrangement could soon be tested at the national level.
Opinion polls put the PP first, followed by Sanchez’s Socialists (PSOE), with Vox third.
The PP is projected to fall short of an outright majority, but together the two right-wing parties are expected to have enough seats to govern.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo has indicated that he would prefer to lead a minority government with Vox’s backing in parliament, while leaving open the possibility of a coalition like the one in Andalusia.
Tucked away between rows of greenhouses and arid mountains in the southern region of Andalusia, Rioja is home to about 1,600 people.
Overlooking the plains framing the quaint village is a giant silhouette of a bull. For much of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship, this area remained poor and largely agricultural.
As machines took over more of the work in the fields, many Andalusians left for jobs in industrial centres such as Barcelona and Madrid. In the mid-seventies, the Socialists found fertile ground in a society that had long felt marginalised and neglected.
In 1982, the PSOE won an absolute majority in Andalusia’s first regional election, beginning a stretch in power that lasted more than three decades.
‘The PP opened the door to the far-right’
But by 2018, the Socialists’ hold on the southern region was starting to crack.
A series of corruption scandals tarnished the party’s image, benefitting the PP. The PSOE still came first in that year’s regional election, but the conservatives took power with the backing of the liberal Ciudadanos and Vox.
It was a turning point.
“For the first time, the PP opened the door to the far-right to be able to govern – that created a precedent for everything that happens today nationwide,” said Bosco Govantes, political science associate professor at Sevilla’s Universidad Pablo de Olavide. “Before, there was a red line, a stigma, over collaborating with the far right. But that move in Andalusia kicked off the normalisation of Vox’s narrative.”
The party was founded in 2013 when a group of ultraconservatives, led by Santiago Abascal, broke up with the conservatives they accused of being too indulgent towards Catalan separatists.
Vox at first struggled to get into the political mainstream, but entered Andalusia’s regional parliament in 2018.
Once the Catalan issue faded from the national debate, the party shifted its focus to migration.
Abascal accuses Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people” as the Socialist government adopted an open-door policy and legalised undocumented migrants who had worked in Spain for years.
Since the start of Sanchez’s rule to last year, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, official figures show. He takes pride in the policy, as Spain’s GDP grew under his tenure.
Vox, the likely kingmaker that is expected to increase its vote share more than any other party compared with the 2023 elections, wants to reverse those policies.
Some observers say the conservative party has had to harden its discourse, such as calling for stricter measures against migrants, to stop haemorrhaging voters to its right.
Polling by Ipsos suggested up to 20 percent of Spaniards who voted for the PP in the 2023 elections intended to vote for Vox on Sunday.
Sanchez has pitched the election as a battle between progress and regression, warning that PP and Vox “only agree when it comes to cutting back rights”.
But that argument falls flat in parts of Andalusia, where some do not fear a Vox-PP deal.
“I don’t mind if Vox is in government,” said Rosaria, a 69-year-old retired housewife, while adjusting her white scarf with a red floral pattern. “The PP will keep them in check. It’s a party with vision and structure”.
Sanchez warns that Vox wants to roll back women’s rights.
The issue of gender violence divides the two parties.
Last year, the PP backed the renewal of Spain’s cross-party pact on gender-based violence.
Vox wants to repeal the 2004 gender-based violence law, which protects women from abuse by current or former partners. The party argues that the law discriminates against men and wants to replace it with legislation covering domestic violence regardless of the victim’s sex.
At an event against gender-based violence, Rioja’s PP mayor Olga Maria Gonzalez Jurado was asked how the two parties were getting on in government in Andalusia.
“I think it’s going well,” she said, but she deflected questions on whether the PP had hardened its stance on immigration to keep up with Vox.

Iranian drone kills 2 Italian Rheinmetall workers in Kuwait
November 26, 2026
An Iranian drone strike on Kuwait left two Italians dead on Thursday, the Italian Foreign Ministry said.
What do we know so far?
The Italians were working for the Italian branch of German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall.
"An explosion caused by a drone attack... occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working," the statement from the Foreign Ministry said.
Kuwait's Defense Ministry said a Kuwaiti and Pakistani national were injured in the "criminal attack" on a "vital site" and taken to the hospital.
Meloni extends 'heartfelt condolences' to victims of families
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she learned of the "tragic" deaths of two Italian citizens in Kuwait during a European Council meeting.
"On behalf of myself and the government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families," Meloni posted on X. "My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also said she was "saddened" by the news.
"We must step up pressure on Iran to put an end to these unacceptable attacks against its neighbors and our partners in the Gulf," von der Leyen said. "Today's events are yet another reminder that security in the Gulf is a matter of security for us all."
Kuwait, a US ally in the Middle East, has been frequently targeted by Iranian attacks since the start of the US-Israeli war against Iran in February.

items.text:
Africa: Opposition voices face growing pressure
November 26, 2026
From Cameroon and Tanzania to Mozambique, Nigeria and Zambia, opposition leaders have accused authorities of limiting political freedoms through legal action and restrictions on public activity.
In each case, officials say the measures are justified under national laws and security provisions.
"Cameroon is very sensitive, and it is important that we know when to criticize the government and when not to criticize the government openly," said Ngam Glory Ani Mbom, a citizen of the Central African country.
She says fear of arrest and violence discourages political participation. "You cannot talk about democracy when opposition supporters cannot freely express their minds to the public," she told DW.
For Nda Grimbald, deputy secretary-general of Cameroon's opposition Social Democratic Front, one of the biggest obstacles is organizing public meetings.
"The first major challenge we face as members of the opposition is the non-authorization of public rallies, public meetings," he told DW, noting that opposition proposals receive little attention in parliament. "Private members' bills are not even listened to."
Cameroonian law guarantees freedom of assembly but allows authorities to restrict gatherings on grounds of public order or national security. Organizers are also required to notify officials in advance.
Tanzania: Trial and prison
In Tanzania, opposition leader Tundu Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason. In November 2026, the High Court acquitted him of treason but convicted him of incitement and sentenced him to four years in prison.
Prosecutors argued that Tundu Lissu's remarks were intended to disrupt Tanzania's 2025 general election. In its ruling, the court said it was satisfied that his statements were intended to "disrupt elections and instigate violence."
Lissu rejected the verdict, calling the case "political persecution." He told the judges: "I was not charged with incitement but you judges are convicting me with it just to impress the person who gives you the titles." He added: "Excuses were created to imprison me."
Gerson Msigwa, Tanzania's chief government spokesperson, directly rejected allegations of political repression and human rights violations.
"Concerns of diminishing civic space and restrictions on political parties to engage in political processes in the lead up to the general election are unfounded and misleading," Msigwa said in response to Amnesty International's accusations of a "wave of terror" sweeping Tanzania ahead of the 2025 vote.
Mozambique: Charges disputed
In Mozambique, opposition figure Venancio Mondlane faces five charges linked to protests after the disputed 2024 election, including incitement to terrorism and public advocacy of crime. Prosecutors accuse him of encouraging violence and civil disobedience. Mondlane denies the allegations.
"I have more than enough evidence. There's plenty to go around. Many of my statements were precisely in the opposite direction," he told DW, adding that the protests were intended to prevent violence.
Pedro Sinai Nhatitima, a judge counselor and spokesperson for Mozambique's Supreme Court, defended the court's decision not to allow live broadcasts of Mondlane's trial. He denied that the proceedings are politically influenced, saying the court will decide the case according to the law.
Nigeria: Policing dissent?
In Nigeria, police in Borno State arrested five men wearing T-shirts bearing the slogan "Tinubu Must Go!" The police say the men were not arrested for their political views, but were found with suspected drugs and other items and face allegations including public disturbance and thuggery.
In Kano, police blocked access to a venue for a planned meeting, citing public safety concerns.
Zambia: Courts and controversy
In Zambia, opposition leader Brian Mundubile has criticized what he describes as a retreat from democratic rights. The courts were closed on August 24, the final day for filing a presidential election petition. The judiciary cited security reasons, while police said intelligence-led security assessments were under way at several government institutions.
State House presidential aide Clayson Hamasaka denied that President Hakainde Hichilema had ordered the closure to prevent an election challenge.
The same month, former opposition lawmaker and cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot dead during a security operation at Mundubile's residence. Authorities said the operation followed intelligence about individuals considered a national security threat, and that officers came under gunfire and returned fire.
Mundubile, who faces treason and sedition charges with other opposition figures, has called for fairness in the proceedings. "We expect an open court process. We are innocent of all the charges against us," he said.
Zambian constitutional lawyer Linda Kasonde has warned: "As you can see, our public institutions are on trial. Democracy in Zambia is on trial."
Cameroonian political analyst Kenang Derek Fay says that despite the setbacks, democratic development across the continent remains a work in progress.
"We are far from getting to the best level," he said. "It is a democracy still struggling to find its way."
DW correspondent Moki Edwin Kindzeka contributed reporting.

Sutton's predictions v Kings of Leon drummer Nathan Followill
- Published
Arsenal co-chairman Josh Kroenke should probably turn his phone off if the Gunners fall behind against Manchester City on Sunday.
Chris Sutton's predictions guest this week, Kings of Leon drummer and City fan Nathan Followill, is good friends with Kroenke - and says he will be in touch if the game is going City's way.
"I'm super excited for this weekend and I've got my smack talk ready for Josh already," Followill told BBC Sport.
"I've heard about the City fans with their inflatable bananas and I need to get myself one. My wife is going to be like 'er, an inflatable banana just arrived in the mail - do you know anything about that?'
"We are going to win 4-2 so I will be texting Josh throughout the game... and, after Erling Haaland's second goal, I will send him a picture of me kissing the banana!"
AI has also made its predictions, and you can pick your own below.
The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.
A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.
Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competition.
Followill has supported City for more than 20 years, external and his children have followed in his footsteps by becoming Blues, despite the best efforts of his next-door neighbour in Nashville, as well as Kroenke.
"When my kids were born, they both received a full Arsenal kit - head to toe - in the mail from Josh," he explained.
"Both times, they were returned to sender - instantly.
"My son and daughter are both City fans now, but my neighbour, Jeremy Connor, is Tottenham, and I mean flying the flag full on.
"When they lose, you can hear him screaming - and when they win, you can hear him screaming too.
"His son is trying to convert my son to Spurs and I am like 'that is never going to happen in this house!'"
Chris Sutton and Nathan Followill were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.
The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Xabi Alonso's side have also lost as many league games - five - as Manchester United, and United are in crisis.
Alonso is not under pressure, or anything like that, but if they lose this game too, you can imagine the mood of the club - and it won't be good.
Apparently their fans were singing 'you don't know what you're doing' at him after their defeat by Leeds - which is what they sang at me when I was there.
Alonso needs to decide on a shape and a way of playing, and stick with it.
Anything could happen here, because Nottingham Forest's form is hardly convincing either.
They tore Manchester City apart in their previous home game, before the international break, but can they really dig out another result like that here?
I think they will go about it in a similar way, and be aggressive and have a real go at Chelsea... and I don't see Chelsea's defence keeping them out.
Sutton's prediction: 2-1
Nathan's prediction: No-one thought Forest would beat us, and while Chelsea need a big result, I can see Forest getting a point here. 1-1
AI's prediction: 1-2
Saturday, 28 November
- Elland Road, 15:00
We talked about Leeds on the Monday Night Club and how they have upgraded their team with the players Daniel Farke bought over the summer.
Farke strengthened in the areas he needed to improve, but is still trusting some of the players who did well for him last season - the likes of Jayden Bogle and James Justin, who have been outstanding.
They are a really well-balanced team and they have good depth to their squad too. The only criticism would be that they are not usually free-scoring - they hit four against Chelsea but before then they had only managed 10 goals in their first 10 league games.
Leeds do not give much away at the back either, though, and I think that will be key in this game.
When I watch Coventry they are dynamic with their counter-attacks and I always fancy them to nick a goal like that.
Not this time, however. Leeds might take a while to break them down, but I think they will come out on top.
Sutton's prediction: 2-0
Nathan's prediction: Coventry play in sky blue too? Part of the reason I became a Manchester City fan was the kit, and I have always gravitated towards teams in light blue, so I am going to go with Coventry here. 0-1

No-one thought it was going to be easy for Mauricio Pochettino to go in at United and turn things around. He has taken over a complete rabble.
United's draw in Lisbon on Wednesday was chaotic, but you also have to consider how Sporting have not got going in the Portuguese league or the Champions League this season.
That was not a great Sporting side. They are pretty average and Brentford will be a much bigger test.

items.text:
A big week for…
Bayern Munich have hit a snagging point, with injuries wracking Vincent Kompany’s squad just as the head coach returns to work following his own health scare. For Lille’s winner, to exact Bayern’s first loss of the season, Aleksandar Pavlović had an own goal for the ages, desperately chasing back to then somehow direct the ball into his own net. Bayern are 15th in the Champions League table, and with Harry Kane out until well into 2027 and 18-year-old Lennart Karl asked to lead the line, resources are stretched. Jamal Musiala, subject of club grandees Uli Hoeness and Karl Heinz-Rummenigge’s gripes over his contract in the light of his neurological condition, could also play only 15 minutes.
Praise instead is due to Lille, coached by Davide Ancelotti to their first win of the group stage. They are captained by 36-year-old Benjamin André, who played one of the best matches of his long career. “Underrated” in the view of Ancelotti, who worked at Bayern under his father, Carlo. “Tonight was something special, we played like a monster.”
Soccer’s world-leading content delivery machine continues to supply a high grade of entertainment. While critics carp against the group stage’s baggy format, Manchester United have supplied the thrills, the spills, the pratfalls. Following the pathos of Atlético Madrid and Como, a comedy of errors at Sporting, with Senne Lammens saving a penalty from Luis Suárez, being unable to save Suárez’s next spot-kick and then dropping the ball for the same player to equalise for a 2-2 scoreline that undersold the chaos. United’s second goal, Bruno Fernandes’s second, also came via farcical means, beating Kaique Pereira, the Sporting keeper, after a bobble off a divot in the Estádio José Alvalade’s surface that Fernandes had himself created when trying to keep his footing. A word, too, for Szymon Marciniak, who gave a strange, overly-fussy referee’s performance, ruling out two seemingly legitimate United goals.
Were United improved? It was difficult to gauge. “With a performance like today it’s the best medicine to prepare the next game,” said Mauricio Pochettino, possibly still jet-lagged yet already deep in the United reeds. His team are 19th in both the Champions League and Premier League.
Kevin De Bruyne’s return to the Etihad brought yearning from both player and former club. Manchester City’s struggles continue and De Bruyne, now 35, is not performing as desired for Napoli, while those from within City continue to push the idea of business as usual amid the limbo of those guilty charges, two empty tiers of the renovated stadium cast telling shadows. Playing in an unfamiliar orange kit for reasons of partnership with a fashion firm best known for football casual “clobber” only added to the surrealism.
“When you don’t win, you question everything,” Erling Haaland said following a 2-2 draw rescued by some Rayan Cherki magic. Among those questions is how Enzo Maresca is dealing with the succession and legacy of Pep Guardiola. Recent signs are unpromising.
Player of the week
In late 2026, the year of Harry Kane, another Englishman is setting controls for the Ballon d’Or. Jude Bellingham has never played a Premier League match but who in the world’s richest league could afford him? At half-time against PSV Eindhoven, Real Madrid were 1-0 down, and then José Mourinho threw on Bellingham. He scored only one of the five his team ran in, though it was spectacular; a volley bearing a light comparison to Madrid legend Zinedine Zidane’s goal in 2002’s final in Glasgow. “I think Zidane is much better than me, he’s much more elegant and he’s my idol,” said a humble Bellingham, while also dismissing talk of inheriting Kane’s crown.
Club in focus: Real Betis
Only their second season in the competition, their previous campaign coming in 2005-06, when Marcos Assunção, Ricardo Oliveira and Joaquín were the star names, Betis are sixth in the table with four wins from five. The knockouts beckon.
The 2026 vintage is full of experience, with Manuel Pellegrini, 73, coaching a team captained by Isco, 34, and still as inventive as ever. The star man in defeating Slovan Bratislava was the Colombian striker Cucho Hernández, previously of Columbus Crew. Two towering headers made sure Slovan remained bottom on zero points.
“I was convinced it was going to be a magical night for me personally,” said Hernández, who was returning after over a month’s absence. Troy Parrott faces a fight to get back in, having been the match-winner in Betis’s opening defeat of Lille. Wednesday was another night where Antony, a Manchester United escapee flourishing elsewhere was a major threat.
They said it
“We don’t need to sign players in the transfer window, it’s not our style to sign a player for just six months. Above all, we’re not afraid of anything. We’re confident in our abilities and our resilience … Are we going to start crying and complaining? No, that’s not how a team operates.” – Paris Saint-Germain’s chances of a third title in succession were lowered when Désiré Doué joined Khvicha Kvaratskheliain the ruptured ACL club. Their coach, Luis Enrique, remains unbowed but Wednesday’s 2-2 draw with Roma suggested certain vulnerabilities. A new-look front three of Maghnes Akliouche, Ferran Torres and Senny Mayulu started against the Serie A club.
Looking ahead
Liverpool, following a 3-0 win at Club Brugge that belied the scoreline, are the highest-ranked English team in the standings in fifth and host Porto next time out. Arsenal, in seventh after their shaky draw with Dortmund on Tuesday, host Real Madrid in two huge Premier League-La Liga summits; Manchester City travel to Barcelona. Two top-eight surprise packages, Betis and Como, also meet.

A bad mistake that gifted Sporting their second goal on Wednesday, having earlier c
items.text:
Lammens - the Man Utd goalkeeper under scrutiny like never before
- Published
After a first season at Manchester United that drew little but praise, goalkeeper Senne Lammens is under the microscope like never before.
A bad mistake that gifted Sporting their second goal on Wednesday, having earlier conceded a clumsy penalty, followed several other errors so far this season.
The 24-year-old Belgium international also made an error at the World Cup in the summer, spilling a shot that led to Spain's winning goal in the 88th minute of their quarter-final.
"I don't know [at what point Manchester United drop him]," legendary Manchester United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel told CBS Sports on Wednesday.
"Mauricio Pochettino has come in and brought his own staff. That means he's got a new goalkeeping coach and maybe that is something that can change it for him.
"[At the World Cup] he came on against Spain and made a bit of a mistake. Mikel Merino scored and they got knocked out. I feel he's lost a little bit of confidence from that mistake and hasn't really recovered.
"As a goalkeeper, when you're not on your best form, you need your defenders in front of you to help you out. The sad truth is that they haven't been able to do that and that makes it so much worse. I like him a lot but today was not a great day for him."
Penalty hero to villain in 75 seconds
Director of football Jason Wilcox and United's data team overruled Ruben Amorim when they opted to sign Lammens from Royal Antwerp for £18.1m in September 2025.
Amorim wanted Argentina World Cup winner Emiliano Martinez, who was left waiting for a deadline day call that never came to seal a move from Aston Villa.
United felt Lammens had the attributes to become one of the world's best goalkeepers. At 24, he is still young. Schmeichel was 27 when he joined United in 1991. Edwin van der Sar was 34 when he left Fulham in 2005. Both had hundreds of senior appearances behind them. Lammens has just over 100, more than half of them with Royal Antwerp.
Although he made the odd error last season, Lammens did nothing to suggest Wilcox and co had got it wrong.
After releasing Turkey international Altay Bayindir, who replaced Andre Onana as first choice at the start of last season and is back on loan in Turkey with Trabzonspor, they signed 36-year-old Wales international Karl Darlow as back-up this term.
Darlow finished last season as first choice at Leeds. But he only started 30 league games in three seasons with the Elland Road outfit. Also on the bench in Lisbon was Tom Heaton. The 40-year-old has not played in a senior game since February 2023.
Mistakes earlier in the season – former United midfielder Paul Scholes claimed in September '"the jury is still out" on whether Lammens is truly top class – have brought increased analysis. His positioning for Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal for Liverpool on Sunday was questioned externally, even if United focused their attentions on Bradley Barcola shoving into the wall.
On Wednesday, it all went wrong.
Just 75 seconds after getting down to make an excellent save from Luis Suarez's first penalty, Lammens recklessly charged out and upended Maxi Araujo, even though Noussair Mazraoui seemed to be in a position to deal with it.
Then, after two Bruno Fernandes goals at the start of the second period had turned the Champions League tie in the visitors' favour, Lammens reached to collect a high ball and inexplicably dropped it in front of Suarez, who applied the overhead kick finish.
Understandably, there was sympathy in the dressing room.
"This team is a family," said striker Joshua Zirkzee. "There's no-one who will suffer by themselves.
"Senne is a great goalkeeper and mistakes happen. In this moment, we just give him space. I'm not sure if he wants to hear anything at all. But Senne's a great kid. He's got a good head on him. We didn't draw because of him, and we all know that next game he is going to be at the top of his game."
Jimenez the key to Lammens bouncing back
Toni Jimenez is Pochettino's long-time goalkeeping coach.
His arrival triggered the exit of Craig Mawson, who had been with Manchester United since 2019. Connor King is Jimenez's assistant but a relative newcomer himself, having joined from Burnley in 2026.
By its nature, goalkeeping at the highest level can be a mental challenge as well as a technical one. As Onana discovered, flaws can quickly become major issues and once the spotlight is shining, the attention is fierce.
Lammens has given the impression privately of being strong. He has seemed remarkably unaffected by his World Cup torment – his mistake against Spain came after he was introduced as a 71st-minute replacement for injured veteran Thibaut Courtois with the quarter-final delicately poised at 1-1. But only he knows the full picture.
Jimenez will be Pochettino's guide over what to do about the situation, although for now, Lammens' head coach is behind him.
"This type of thing happens," he said. "That is football. Football is about making mistakes.
"I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.
"It's not to blame the defensive line, but it's two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better."
Lammens and defence must both improve
Following Wednesday's draw in Lisbon, Pochettino highlighted "two things" that need to improve if United are to start winning matches on a regular basis.
The first of those is the club's preferred goalkeeper. Of the 17 Premier League goalkeepers to have played a minimum of 10 matches in all competitions in this campaign, Lammens has the second-worst save success rate, keeping out just 60.2% of the shots he has faced. Only Coventry's Carl Rushworth (54.4%) has fared worse so far this season.

From leadership crises to tech outages, can corporations rebuild public trust?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

From cyberattacks to network failures to leadership crises, tech corporations are showing signs of vulnerability. The dramatic resignation and return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has underscored the potential risk of depending on a single leader, both for the company and the entire AI industry. Meanwhile, global outages at Microsoft and a number of US banks have showcased declining public trust in institutions.
Read moreWhat we know about Microsoft's widespread outages that caused global chaos
Allyson Stewart-Allen, CEO of International Marketing Partners, says the scandal at Nvidia has put a spotlight on tech firms that are dependent on a single leader. "From a governance point of view and from a brand point of view, this is a very risky strategy to just be beholden to one individual. Whether it's Steve Jobs or Sam Altman or Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg (...) I would have thought if you were an investor, a customer and potentially a regulator, you would be quite concerned about the risk that you have by putting all your eggs in this one basket."
She says that corporate governance at Nvidia will also be under scrutiny. "It begs the question, what other influences could Nvidia be exposed to from other outside influencers? (...) And in terms of the brand and trust in the Nvidia brand, I think the question is, does the board govern this company responsibly?"
Stewart-Allen warns that the tech industry in particular faces an uphill climb to rebuild consumer and regulator trust. "How they do that is a function of solid leaders, explicit communication, reassurance that the past offences and transgressions have been addressed and won't happen again (...) We are looking for companies to trust."

items.text:
Freigang banned — Germany star to miss 2027 World Cup
November 26, 2026
Laura Freigang is set to miss next year's women's World Cup in Brazil after being suspended for missing doping tests, the German Football Association (DFB) said in a statement on Thursday.
Freigang, who has 45 Germany caps and scored 17 goals, will be suspended until October 7, 2027 after reaching a settlement with the DFB, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and Germany's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA). The suspension is for the next 16-months as it began retroactively on June 8, 2026, when she was notified by the DFB.
"It's important to me to emphasize once again that I was never suspected of doping," Freigang said in a statement on Instagram.
"My agreement to a settlement does not mean that I share all the assessments of my case. The past few months have been extremely difficult for me. Another legal process would have entailed significant financial, mental, and emotional strain. This is why I decided to take this path, in the hope of finding some peace, clarity, and perspective for myself," she added.
"It was never my intention to let it get this far. Sports have defined my life since I was little. It breaks my heart that, for now, I won't be able to step onto the field, help my team, or live the daily life that I love so much."
End of an ongoing process for Freigang
This brings to a close a case that has been ongoing for months. The 28-year-old had been accused of not being where she said she would be for a doping control on three occasions between March 2025 and February 2026.
In June of this year, Freigang explained missing the tests "were not deliberately avoided appointments but inconsistencies or misunderstandings in the comprehensive details that have to be updated daily and which we as national team players have to update in the system on a daily and hourly basis."
The ban ends her World Cup hopes, something the DFB has also acknowledged.
"We are simply so sorry for Laura on a personal level because of this situation. The past few weeks have been very stressful for her," said DFB Sporting Director Nia Künzer. "We hold her in high regard both as a player and as a person, and—as we have done in recent weeks—we will continue to stay in touch with her and support her as best we can."
The situation also puts her future at her club, Eintracht Frankfurt, into question. Freigang's contract runs until June next year.
"The agreement that has now been reached provides clarity and planning certainty through a process that is unique to Eintracht Frankfurt—for us as a club, but above all for Laura," Katharina Kiel, Frankfurt's director of women's football.
The club and Freigang, who has played 180 Bundesliga games in her career, are now set to enter talks to determine the shape of her contract moving forward.

"FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorized access
items.text:
FIFA says cyberattack against it accessed a 'limited' set of data
November 26, 2026
FIFA told news agencies on Thursday that it had been targeted by a person or group seeking access to its data.
"FIFA can confirm that it has been the victim of a criminal cyberattack resulting in unauthorized access to a limited set of personal and business information," a FIFA spokesperson told the Reuters news agency, issuing similar comments to other outlets.
Reuters cited a person "with direct knowledge of the matter" as saying that less than 0.1% of FIFA's total data had been compromised.
This person also said that no files from the controversial, abandoned FIFA Forward Enterprise project that looked to sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors had been accessed.
What else did FIFA say about the cyberattack?
FIFA said that it was working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement, in the aftermath of the event.
It did not say when the attack took place, list the precise nature of the compromised data or specify how unauthorized access to FIFA data had been sought, amid reports of people having posed as FIFA officials rather than actually hacking the organization or otherwise compromising its cybersecurity systems.
"FIFA condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data," the Zurich-based organization said. "Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned."
Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot of what it said were FIFA files. Three days later, it appeared to take credit for the cyberattack when responding to a post saying that more than 12 gigabytes of internal documents had been posted.
FIFA did not explicitly state whether it was talking about the same supposed incident.
The breach comes at a sensitive time for the organization. Still reeling from the scandalfollowing this summer's World Cup of its now-aborted plans to sell off World Cup commercial rights shares, it's now trying to secure another term for its embattled president, Gianni Infantino.
Infantino is the favorite for an election on March 18, when he is expected toface challenges from Kohzo Tashima of Japan and Philippe Diallo of France. But until the turbulence of the last six months, it seemed most likely he would simply stand unopposed and extend his 11-year tenure without a fight.

items.text:
Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
- Published
French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.
Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".
Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.
But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).
Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.
Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line.

A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.
Re
items.text:
Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
- Published
A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.
The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.
She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.
Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.
The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.
The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.
"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.
All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.
However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.
The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.
