Jamie Carragher felt Man Utd were 'unlucky' to be controversially denied two goals by refereeing decisions and said Mauricio Pochettino will feel like his side were 'robbed' of what would have been a 'really b
items.text:
Man Utd goalkeeper Senne Lammens criticised for howler in Sporting draw by Jamie Carragher
Jamie Carragher felt Man Utd were 'unlucky' to be controversially denied two goals by refereeing decisions and said Mauricio Pochettino will feel like his side were 'robbed' of what would have been a 'really big win'
Thursday 26 November 2026 00:09, UK
Jamie Carragher says Manchester United goalkeeper Senne Lammens' confidence is a cause for concern after his howler cost Mauricio Pochettino a first win since taking charge.
It was a nightmare performance for Lammens, who unnecessarily gave away the penalty for Luis Suarez's opener just 75 seconds after saving the Sporting striker's poorly taken first spot-kick.
Lammens, 24, then spilled a routine cross late in the second half which allowed Suarez to equalise for 2-2, denying United a first away win of the season and first away Champions League win for five years.
The Belgium international, signed from Club Brugge last summer, restored calm between the sticks last season after Andre Onana's calamitous spell as No 1, but has had a poor start to his second season at Old Trafford.

Delivering his verdict on Lammens' performance, Carragher said on CBS: "You worry about the confidence of that goalkeeper now.
"That mistake for the equaliser, the 2-2 goal, you say sometimes 'an amateur goalkeeper wouldn't make that mistake'. If that was an amateur goalkeeper you'd be thinking 'that can't happen'. That just can't happen at this level."
Carragher questioned if United had the options in their goalkeeper department to bring Lammens out of the spotlight for a brief while.
Pochettino could call on Karl Darlow if he wanted to make a change at goalkeeper. He was signed in the summer on a free transfer from Leeds, where he was the No 1 for the second half of last season.
"It is getting to the stage with the goalkeeper now," Carragher added. "The focus on a Man Utd goalkeeper is always big if he's making mistakes. I don't think the back-up's even at the level where, no matter how poorly the goalkeeper plays, you change it."
Carra: Poch will feel Man Utd were robbed
Carragher felt United were "unlucky" to see two goals controversially ruled out but criticised the players for allowing games to spiral out of control when they suffer set-backs.
The Sky Sports pundit said it must frustrate Pochettino but will make for an "unbelievable" watch when the fly-on-the-wall documentary being filmed this season is released.
"Why do they keep shooting themselves in the foot?" said Carragher. "As a manager, what can he really do about the goalkeeper or Tielemans making a stupid tackle at the end?
"He'll be really frustrated because that could have been a really big result for them tonight at 2-1, and there were unlucky with the 3-2 [goal being disallowed].
"He will feel they've been robbed by the referee and he'll say they should have won the game.
"But he'll be looking at isolated incidents and it feels like every game is mad. There's never a normal game where you win 1-0 or you draw 1-1 and nothing really happens. Something happens all the time that you're almost laughing at, or you've got your head in your hands if you're a Man Utd fan.
"There is always madness or craziness. I mean, the documentary is going to be unbelievable isn't it."
Were Man Utd hard done by to have two goals ruled out?
The last thing Pochettino needed after the 4-0 defeat at Liverpool - and Leny Yoro's now overturned red card - was more refereeing controversy. However, there was contention around both goals United had ruled out in Lisbon.
Amad had the ball in the back of the net toward the end of the first half to equalise - but not before the whistle had gone for what was judged to have been a foul by Tielemans, who clearly won the ball with his slide tackle.
The United midfielder received a booking for his follow through on Sporting defender Inacio, who went down dramatically despite receiving the slightest of contact. VAR could not intervene as the whistle had gone.
Morrison, who said Tielemans "won the ball", was adamant that it was the wrong call.
United's second disallowed goal, which was ruled out following VAR intervention, saw Dorgu penalised for making contact with Sporting goalkeeper Kaique before he punched into his own net.
Carragher felt it was "very harsh" for the referee to disallow the goal after being sent to his monitor.

items.title: Championship roundup: Stoke rise to second, Birmingham condemn Burnley to record drought
items.summary:
George Hirst scored both goals as Stoke secured a fifth successive Championship win by beating Millwall 2-1 to go level on points with Middlesbrough at the top.
The Scotland international scored his second goal for the Potters in the 1-0 win over Birmingham on Saturday and doubled his tally for the
items.text:
George Hirst scored both goals as Stoke secured a fifth successive Championship win by beating Millwall 2-1 to go level on points with Middlesbrough at the top.
The Scotland international scored his second goal for the Potters in the 1-0 win over Birmingham on Saturday and doubled his tally for the season to take Stoke back into the automatic promotion places.
Mark Sykes’s stunning strike halved the deficit in the final 10 minutes, but Stoke held on to claim an 11th win in their past 14 outings. The defeat was Millwall’s fourth in a row, coming a day after it was announced they had been ordered to play a future match in front of a partially closed stadium for offensive chanting.
“There’s been a little bit said about George that is unfair,” said the Stoke manager, Mark Robins. “It’s amazing if you just remember that you love playing football and you just go and do it, everything else tends to fall into place. It’s not as simple as that but it really helps, and he’s done that.”
Burnley set a new record for the longest home run without a league win as Birmingham reaffirmed their promotion credentials with a 2-0 victory at Turf Moor thanks to August Priske’s strike and Jaydon Banel’s own goal.
It is now 24 games since Burnley last earned three points in front of their own fans, a nightmare run that has now stretched to 403 days. It represents the worst sequence in the history of English football.
Burnley, relegated from the Premier League last season, remain in the drop zone, one point above the bottom side Derby. Fabio Celestini has picked up three points in the five games he has taken charge of since succeeding Nicky Hayen last month and his team were jeered off at the end. For Birmingham, it was a timely return to form after a 1-0 defeat at Stoke. Chris Davies’s team are two places and two points off the automatic promotion spots.
Watford’s new head coach, Edward Iordanescu, watched from the stands as Todd Cantwell’s penalty condemned the struggling hosts to a 1-0 defeat by resilient Blackburn. The former Romania national team manager, who had just flown in after signing a contract, was introduced to a sparsely populated Vicarage Road to polite applause, 10 minutes before kick-off.
On the evidence of Watford’s third home defeat of the season, he will have his work cut out to steer them away from the Championship’s relegation quicksands.
The Norwegian duo Aune Heggebø and Felix Horn Myhre scored the goals as West Brom boosted their promotion push with a 3-1 win at Bolton. Heggebø gave James Morrison’s in-form visitors the lead which was cancelled out by Ruben Rodrigues’s second-half penalty.
But West Brom, without their injured top scorer Isaac Price, finished strongly, with Myhre’s fifth goal since his summer move from Brann restoring West Brom’s lead after 75 minutes. Heggebø, back in the starting lineup after Saturday’s draw with Swansea, sealed a fifth win in eight games with a penalty.
“I thought [Heggebø] would be perfect for this game if we could get behind their high back line,” said Morrison. On Price’s absence, the West Brom manager added: “Any team would miss big players and what they bring to the team. But it’s not to cry about, it is about trying to find the best way and trust in the players who come in.”

items.title: S&P considers Nvidia credit downgrade over governance and ‘key man’ risks
items.summary:
S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.
Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns
items.text:
S&P Global Ratings, one of the three major credit rating agencies, is considering downgrading Nvidia’s rating, citing concerns about the company’s management and governance practices.
Despite Nvidia’s strong financial performance, the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang has raised concerns about “weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning” and “key man risk,” meaning heavy reliance on Huang for its future success, S&P said in a statement.
The agency expects to finish its review within 90 days and could cut Nvidia’s rating from AA to AA-, the fourth-highest on its scale.
Although Nvidia is certain to keep its investment-grade rating, a downgrade could raise its borrowing costs. Because Nvidia backstops neoclouds and other infrastructure companies that lack strong credit on their own, a lower rating could make their debt costlier or force them to post more collateral.
In August, Nvidia announced plans to arrange $500 billion in financing for AI infrastructure with six financial institutions, including Goldman Sachs, Apollo, and Blackstone. Under the original terms, Nvidia would guarantee 25% of the loans. But even before Huang’s ouster and return, lenders had been demanding that Nvidia guarantee more, Bloomberg reported.
A downgrade would likely prompt lenders to demand even larger guarantees.

items.title: Lammens howler costs Manchester United victory in frantic finale at Sporting
items.summary:
“We are a strong team,” Mauricio Pochettino exhorted, then saw Manchester United’s unerring ability to cause drama each and every time they lace their boots up.
Cruising, it seemed, at 2-1 and with 10 minutes left, they unravelled, as Senne Lammens dropped a regulation high ball in front of his goal
items.text:
“We are a strong team,” Mauricio Pochettino exhorted, then saw Manchester United’s unerring ability to cause drama each and every time they lace their boots up.
Cruising, it seemed, at 2-1 and with 10 minutes left, they unravelled, as Senne Lammens dropped a regulation high ball in front of his goal and a grateful Luis Suárez produced a bicycle kick for the equaliser. Cut almost instantly to Sporting’s Kaique Pereira who bundled the ball in for United’s apparent third only for Szymon Marciniak to be ordered to the screen by the video assistant referee, where the referee ruled the goal out for a foul on the goalkeeper. Even worse Youri Tielemans, in stoppage time, was sent off.
Before this United had come from 1-0 behind and were heading for a first victory under Pochettino and only a fourth of this troubled campaign that would have rewarded the 2,597 travelling fans.
But, after the humiliation at Anfield, victory eluded them. Yet, at least, United did draw. Pochettino can build from this – and will have to, as his players remain a jumble of disjointedness and show far too few moments of incisiveness.
Could United control the contest? In the first half, not really, was the answer as the hooped shirts went at them, Lammens’ miscontrol pointing to a familiar tentativeness. Paulo Fonseca’s team went close, too, when an easy raid down the visitors’ left ended with the ball dropping on Maximiliano Araújo’s left boot but he skied over. Over their previous eight games United had been shown four red cards: for Leny Yoro (twice), Lisandro Martínez and Matheus Cunha. While Yoro’s in Sunday’s 4-0 debacle at Liverpool was rescinded, to average a sending-off every two matches since 13 October pointed to the disarray in the ranks Pochettino had to end.
He reacted to the Anfield horror-show by dropping Matthijs de Ligt for Harry Maguire, one of four changes that featured Joshua Zirkzee starting (in this competition for the first time) at centre-forward for the suspended Cunha.
The Dutchman blasted a chance over from close range – a sign of his sub-elite quality. When Pochettino, whose shape was 4-2-3-1, also witnessed Amad Diallo fail to go at his man along the right, Yoro dawdle in the centre circle, and Kobbie Mainoo pass straight to Issa Doumbia to allow Sporting to turn United, he saw, too, the scale of the work before him.
Now came more serious farce from those in blue. Martínez lost Geny Catamo, scrambled across to his left-back zone in United’s area to challenge, the No 10 went down, and Szymon Marciniak awarded the penalty. Sporting’s 14-goal No 9, Luis Suárez, stepped up but hit the ball straight at Lammens. A turning point in United’s horrendous campaign? Erm, no.
Because moments later Araújo twisted past United’s goalkeeper and was barged over for a second spot-kick. Here, Lammens was lucky to escape a red card, as Araújo had turned possession towards goal, and this time Suárez did score as United’s haplessness continued.
And, ill luck. Because even when Diallo scored what appeared to be the equaliser, Marciniak, oddly, blew for a foul by Youri Tielemans on Gonçalo Inácio just before the finish (so no video assistant referee enquiry was allowed), the midfielder seeming to do nothing apart from play his teammate in.
This had Pochettino and his team raging, an emotion that continued until the break, Tielemans again having it out with Marciniak. The wider picture, though, concerned Pochettino’s pre-match insistence of a lack of fragility. Understandable, maybe, as he could not tell reporters otherwise. But, after the PR, came the evidence of another 45 minutes in which his new charges were hardly robust.
One more mountain to climb, then, in the second period against the 21-times Portuguese champions, who were led by Fonseca in only his third game in charge since being prised from Lyon for roughly £4.5m compensation.
Five minutes after the break, United were in rude health as they pulled ahead. First, a marauding Martínez was fouled by Eduardo Quaresma and Marciniak awarded the night’s third penalty, which Fernandes converted for the first goal of the Pochettino era. Then, the captain scored his second, this time his speculative left-foot shot from just outside the area hitting a divot in front of Kaique Pereira, bouncing over the goalkeeper and in.
Fortune, at last, smiled on United, whose riposte since half-time certainly showed the backbone their head coach asserts they have.
On 65 minutes he made a move, as Patrick Dorgu and Diogo Dalot came on, Bryan Mbeumo becoming the centre-forward. Zirkzee, again, had disappointed – the tale of his United career.
At this juncture United were a yard quicker, more streetwise: the corollary of a surging confidence and belief. On 77 minutes Diallo was forced off, Shea Lacey replacing him. Now, though, came the latest chaos to engulf Pochettino’s side.

items.title: Isak and Wirtz on target as resurgent Liverpool sweep aside Club Brugge
items.summary: Liverpool brought Club Brugge’s impressive run in the Champions League to an abrupt halt on a bitterly cold night in Belgium with an exhibition of outstanding finishing and composed defending. Alexander Isak took his tally for the season into double figures and Florian Wirtz maintained his fine form
items.text:
Liverpool brought Club Brugge’s impressive run in the Champions League to an abrupt halt on a bitterly cold night in Belgium with an exhibition of outstanding finishing and composed defending. Alexander Isak took his tally for the season into double figures and Florian Wirtz maintained his fine form by scoring for a third successive club game. Andoni Iraola’s side are building momentum at the right time.
Isak struck an excellent brace to move to ten goals for the season while Liverpool’s clean sheet will also have encouraged Iraola against a previously free-scoring Brugge team.
This was the first meeting between the clubs since Kenny Dalglish decided the European Cup final with an exquisite chip at Wembley in 1978. Their only other encounters were also in a European final – the two-legged Uefa Cup final in 1976 that Liverpool won 4-3 on aggregate – when Brugge fans adopted You’ll Never Walk Alone as an anthem. Liverpool were made to feel at home as both sets of supporters joined in with a rendition before kick-off. Brugge’s hospitality extended further as their visitors were gifted an early lead.
The early exchanges were evenly matched but Liverpool were handed the initiative courtesy of a needless mistake from veteran goalkeeper Yann Sommer. The former Switzerland international was under no pressure when misplacing a pass intended for defender Brandon Mechele to Bradley Barcola. Barcola simply released Dominik Szoboszlai free inside the area and Liverpool’s captain for the night, with Virgil van Dijk rested on the bench as he was at LASK, squared for Alexander Isak. The striker prodded the ball between the legs of the 37-year-old keeper.
Brugge were as energetic and as aggressive in the press as Iraola had predicted, though Liverpool handled them reasonably well in the first half. Nicolò Tresoldi headed a corner from Felix Lemaréchal beyond Alisson but Szoboszlai was well placed to clear in front of the line. Lemaréchal should have done better when found unmarked at the far post by the captain Hans Vanaken but steered a tame header straight at Alisson. Other Brugge chances fell to defenders Joaquin Seys and Mechele. Szoboszlai, his right knee heavily strapped up, launched himself in the way of the former’s shot and the latter miscued in front of goal from Vanaken’s ball.
Liverpool created few clear openings before the interval yet there were more promising signs from Barcola as his sharpness and speed improves after a pre-season stalled by his move to Merseyside. The France international combined well with Florian Wirtz to set up Isak for a volley that flashed wide of Sommer’s goal and was a constant outlet on the left.
The visitors suffered an injury setback late in the first half when Victor Muñoz collided into Jorne Spileers at the end of a surging run into the Brugge penalty area. Muñoz fouled Spileers when the defender stepped across to cut out the danger but came off worse in the challenge and appeared to damage his knee. The Liverpool winger received lengthy treatment before declining the option of a stretcher and limping off gingerly. Like Barcola he had worked tirelessly before being forced out of the game.
Muñoz’s replacement, Rio Ngumoha, did not take long to make his presence felt and continue the menacing form that helped dismantle Manchester United on Sunday. Receiving possession on the left of the home penalty area, the teenager weaved away from two defenders before curling a shot around a third and wide of the far post.
Liverpool went even closer to a second goal when carving open the Brugge defence with a flowing, incisive move that deserved a fitting reward. Wirtz picked out Isak with a sweeping pass into the box. The striker cushioned his touch into the path of the incoming Szoboszlai and his first-time shot was destined for the far corner only for Sommer to redeem himself with a superb save at full stretch.
Sommer’s save provided a platform for Brugge to enjoy their most sustained spell of pressure in the contest. Liverpool’s central defensive pairing of Jérémy Jacquet and Ronald Araújo coped comfortably with a usually potent forward line, however. Alisson was not seriously troubled until the 70th minute when he met a snap-shot from Lemaréchal with a fine stop at his near post.
Just as home hopes were growing, Liverpool extinguished them with a devastating counterattack from a loose Brugge ball on the edge of their area. Ngumoha led the charge down the right, showing good strength to shrug off Carlos Forbs and then good awareness to find Wirtz unmarked on the opposite flank. The German playmaker controlled on the edge of the box, gave Sommer the eyes, and swept home an excellent finish off the inside of the keeper’s right-hand post.
Minutes later Isak added to the showreel when racing clear on goal after Mechele had slipped as the pair competed for Alisson’s quick clearance. The Sweden international advanced on Sommer’s goal and lifted an impudent chip over the goalkeeper to cap a mature and clinical display from Iraola’s team.

Sporting 2-2 Man Utd: Mauricio Pochettino denied first win by Senne Lammens howler in Champions League
Report as Man Utd self-destruct in bizarre Champions League draw at Sporting after having two goals controversially ruled out; Bruno Fernandes and Luis Suarez both scored two goals, one penalty each, with the Man Utd captain's second goal freakishly bouncing in off a divot in the ground
Wednesday 25 November 2026 22:15, UK
Mauricio Pochettino was denied a first victory as Manchester United head coach by a goalkeeping howler from Senne Lammens in an incident-packed 2-2 draw with Sporting in the Champions League as Youri Tielemans was sent off late on.
United looked to be on course for a first away win of the season after captain Bruno Fernandes scored two goals in the first five minutes of the second half only for Lammens to spill the ball in the box for Luis Suarez to equalise with his second goal of the game.
Pochettino thought United had gone back in front for a second time shortly after Lammens' error when Sporting goalkeeper Kaique punched into his own net at a corner. However, it was ruled out following an on-field review for a foul by substitute Patrick Dorgu.
It was a damaging night for Lammens, who gave away the penalty for Suarez's first goal just 75 seconds after saving the Sporting striker's poorly taken spot-kick. The man brought into replace the error-prone Andre Onana is now beginning to resemble his predecessor.

Fernandes' equaliser three minutes after the restart came from the third penalty of what was a bizarre match. Few moments topped the United skipper's freakish second goal which came thanks a tame effort bouncing up off a divot in the ground and into back of the net.

Pochettino's first two matches have seen his side have two players sent off and concede two penalties. If he did not know it before, he certainly knows now that nothing comes easy at United, who sit 19th in the Champions League and Premier League.
Carra: Man Utd 'unlucky' but Lammens error can't happen
Sky Sports pundit Jamie Carragher to CBS:
"I do think United were a little bit unlucky tonight with the goal disallowed just before half-time. The goal at the end felt very harsh to me, the one where it could have been 3-2...
"The focus on a Man Utd goalkeeper is always big if he's making mistakes. The back-ups aren't even at the level where you could say no matter how poorly the goalkeeper plays, you could change it. You worry about the confidence of that goalkeeper now.

Poch praises Man Utd 'personality'
Man Utd head coach Mauricio Pochettino to TNT Sports:
"I'm so proud of the players. It was a tough game. I liked the team we played for 90 minutes, the personality, the character. It's difficult to find a game where you get punished in one game. We were punished a lot in key actions. Today we showed how we want to play after just one week of working together.
"We need to concentrate and focus more, try to recover better. The performance like today's is the best medicine to prepare for the next game."

items.title: Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
items.summary: Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an
items.text:
Last year, Google filed a patent for a system called My Channel that’s designed to create feeds filled with personalized, AI-generated videos and advertisements based on information the company knows about its users. The patent has been rejected, but unfortunately, Google might appeal or resubmit an amended version, and we could see this monstrosity come to market.
Google’s patent for custom AI video feeds paints a bleak picture of entertainment’s future
Imagine an endless feed of AI slop in which you are the main character of every story.
First spotted by Patentlyze, the patent — which was filed last May and published last week — describes how My Channel would use a person’s demographic data and viewing history to create its own prompts that would then be fed into an LLM to help generate AI videos tailored to that person’s specific interests. In addition to factoring in what kinds of videos a user tends to watch, the system would capture contextual data from their device like IP addresses, GPS locations, and specific details about the user’s age. My Channel could also base its prompts on current news like sports scores and things happening on social media, and all of the video generation would take place on Google’s servers.
According to the patent, My Channel would be able to churn out entire movies of various genres. If a user watches a lot of videos about Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, the system might serve up something like Ash Koosha’s Odysseus: The Fall. The patent details how My Channel might be able to connect to other streaming services — which would give it even more information about users and, presumably, access to useful training data for video generation. It all seems like a convoluted way to whip up AI knockoffs of professionally produced art, but what’s most unsettling about the patent are its mentions of My Channel creating digital avatars of users and turning them into “the protagonist or lead character” in the content it pumps out.
Setting aside the fact that My Channel would use photos, videos, and audio clips of people to create these avatars, the system sounds like it is designed to generate a form of “entertainment” that is deeply at odds with what makes engaging with art a worthwhile, enjoyable experience. It can be fun to metaphorically project one’s self into fictional narratives to understand how characters feel, but what Google is proposing is giving people access to an endless supply of bespoke content that doesn’t at all encourage them to use their imaginations to empathize with or relate to the characters. The patent makes it seem like Google thinks that viewers would be entertained enough just by seeing themselves onscreen. That’s bleak in and of itself because My Channel sounds very much like an unholy cross between JibJab and the panoptic elements of Google.
My Channel feels like an even more depressing idea when you consider how the service would make it that much easier for its users to avoid broadening their horizons by being exposed to new things that exist outside their comfort zones. If Google were able to strike the right licensing deals with other streaming services, My Channel users could presumably gorge themselves on artless AI regurgitations of preexisting content. That might keep some people glued to the service — a goal that every streaming platform strives for — but it would also discourage them from engaging with entertainment that isn’t expressly crafted to appeal to their assumed tastes.
When people refer to AI-generated videos as “slop,” they’re talking about the fact that generative models are incapable of generating art with the same kind of creative intention that makes human-made stories compelling. Video generation models can mimic visual elements of the data (read: movies and series) they’re trained on, but they cannot truly think or feel in the way that directors, writers, and actors can. This reality is why it has been so baffling to see AI-boosting entertainment companies, streamers, and studios insisting that the technology will fundamentally revolutionize the industry for the better. It feels much more likely that gen AI is going to keep flooding the internet with garbage no one wants to watch.

Research artifact. Not maintained and not accepting contributions.
A Lean 4 proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the Generalized Riemann
Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, built on Mathlib and using only the
axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
The proof is based on Levent Alpöge's, with Claude (https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf). This repository is a shorter version, produced in collaboration with my colleagues at Anthropic, and Claude.
- grh/: readable edition, about 300,000 lines. Start at grh/GUIDE.md.
- grh-compact/: the same five theorems, about 76,000 lines.
Each folder is its own Lake project with its own README.
Needs Lean v4.35.0 and Mathlib at commit 56a00585. In either folder:
lake exe cache get
lake build
lake env lean scripts/PrintAxioms.lean
A build takes one to two hours on 12 cores with 24 GB of memory (about 85 minutes more if the Mathlib cache is missing).
The proof has passed machine checks only, listed in each folder's README. No mathematician has read it through, and no paper comes with it.

Ferguson's Glentoran reign hits early turbulence
- Published
If Duncan Ferguson is to be a success at Glentoran, it will be without the benefit of any new manager bounce.
The former Everton striker arrived at the Oval in October amid plenty of fanfare and sparked hopes that the high-profile left-fie
items.text:
Ferguson's Glentoran reign hits early turbulence
- Published
If Duncan Ferguson is to be a success at Glentoran, it will be without the benefit of any new manager bounce.
The former Everton striker arrived at the Oval in October amid plenty of fanfare and sparked hopes that the high-profile left-field appointment would be the one to lead the Glens to a first Irish Premiership title since 2009.
However, under the Scot the east Belfast outfit have struggled for results, registering just one win in five matches, and exited the BetMcLean Cup after being beaten at home by Larne on Tuesday night.
On top of their inconsistent form, Ferguson was handed a seven-game suspension following a red card for arguing with officials in the side's 3-2 defeat by Cliftonville last week and will not be back in the dugout until 2027.
'We'll just have to accept it and get on with it' - Morris
Earning his first Irish Premiership red card in just his fourth match in charge was an unwanted milestone for Ferguson but it is the resulting suspension that poses a more significant problem.
The 1995 FA Cup winner was dismissed for the way he addressed match officials after believing the Reds' opener at Solitude should have been ruled out for a foul in the build-up.
Ferguson has since apologised but will now miss a string of key games including the highly anticipated 'Big Two' Boxing Day derby, a match that may not require much of a team talk from the manager but is perhaps biggest single fixture in the Irish Premiership calendar.
While Ferguson must watch his new team from the stands, assistant coach Gary Bollan will take charge with the help of goalkeeping coach Elliot Morris.
"Yeah, I think it's a big miss for us in the changing room, not having his voice and not having his persona in the changing room," Morris said when asked about Ferguson's ban.
"He's a big character, but it is what it is and we'll just have to accept it and get on with it.
"He's accepted it, the club's accepted it, we'll just get on with it and try and focus for the second Larne match."
Could Weatherup be key for the Glens?
Following Declan Devine's departure in September, results under interim manager Paddy McCourt and coach Tim McCann suggested that the Glens may be beginning to turn a corner, but Ferguson has so far found it difficult to build upon that progress.
Five points from four games in the Irish Premiership, now paired with the setback of a cup exit, shows that there is plenty for Ferguson to address.
Victory over Bangor remains the highlight of the new manager's tenure to date, but even that win was only secured thanks to Cal Weatherup's 87th-minute winner.
Indeed, the upturn in form of striker Weatherup has been one bright point for the side in recent weeks.
After limited minutes at the start of the season, the 18-year-old has now netted three goals in his past three games.
His emergence is particularly welcome given leading striker Pat Hoban continues to work his way back from injury and former Northern Ireland international Conor McMenamin looks to recapture his best form after returning to the Irish Premiership in the summer.
Ferguson will know the importance of the Glens looking like more of a threat in the final third and one of his aims will be to help the former Glentoran academy forward continue his recent form and bolster the east Belfast side's front-line.
Ferguson will surely have already seen enough to start on his plans to help the Glens end their long wait for Premiership success - even if he is to be watching the next six games from a frustrating remove.
His personality and contacts are still to be major assets for the Glens and he can continue to put his stamp on the side during training.
Ferguson has already signed one player during his time at the club - free agent Nathan Shaw - but the January transfer window will give him the opportunity to bring in further fresh faces.
The Glens sit in fourth and 17 points behind league leaders Linfield in the Premiership, but there will be another chance to seal silverware in the form of the Irish Cup, a competition they have won 23 times.
By the time Glentoran come into that competition in January, Ferguson will finally be back in dugout rather than the director's box.
Ferguson's tenure will not be defined by these early days, but he is experienced enough to know that a quick upturn in results is crucial.
For now, all attention turns to Friday's Irish Premiership rematch against the Inver Reds - live on BBC iPlayer - as Ferguson's side look to get their season back on track without him on the sidelines.

items.summary:
At least 30 killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
- Published
At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.
Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and
items.text:
At least 30 killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
- Published
At least 30 people have been killed and 19 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.
Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.
Unverified footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.
Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.
The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.
The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.
It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.
Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.
The health ministry said 39 ambulances had been dispatched to respond to the fire, while it posted images of Egypt's health minister overseeing the treatment of the injured at one of Cairo's hospitals.
Road collisions are also common in Egypt, often attributed to lax maintenance and the widespread flouting of traffic laws.
Nearly 6,000 people died on Egypt's roads last year, official figures show, a rise of several hundred on the previous year's total.
Emergency responders have since cleared the highway and allowed it to reopen, state broadcaster NMA reports.
A bulldozer could earlier be seen at the scene clearing the burnt-out wrecks of cars.

items.summary: The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and
items.text:
The New York Times is asking freelance photographers not to use the newest version of Adobe Photoshop because features in the 2027 update use AI “in ways that may not be apparent to users.” In an email seen by The Verge and posted on Threads, two of the Times’ photography leaders, Meaghan Looram and Josh Haner, write that the use of these features “can result in metadata identifying photographs as AI-generated.”
The New York Times warns photographers not to update Photoshop over AI features
An email sent to freelance photographers says Photoshop’s latest update uses AI ‘in ways that may not be apparent.’
Adobe has spent the past few years filling Photoshop and other apps in its creative suite with a trove of AI-powered tools. The November update cited by the NYT’s email adds several new AI features, including Adobe’s new “AI Assisted Editor” view, which lets users access all of Photoshop’s AI features from a single toolbar. It also adds an AI assistant for step-by-step editing instructions, prompt-based image transformation and editing, new AI upscaling options, and an AI-powered tool that recomposes images for different canvas sizes.
It’s not always clear which tools in Adobe’s apps are AI-powered, and even some older options like automated selection tools may now be considered part of the AI suite. This can lead to photos ending up with metadata indicating they were edited with AI, which is a blunt way of describing what happened in post-production. For a newsroom like the Times, where photo editing is kept to a minimum, the metadata risks losing readers’ trust. Last year, the Times said that it does not “retouch or digitally manipulate” photos but may “make minimal adjustments to color to ensure we are accurately reproducing the image.”
In August, Adobe began rolling out support for C2PA metadata across its apps, which indicates whether an image is AI-generated or edited using AI features. The NYT is issuing its restriction to keep these tags from inadvertently appearing in its photos. “At this time, we are requiring that all contributing photographers avoid using Adobe Photoshop 2027 (release 28.0.0 and subsequent updates) when working on assignment for The Times,” the email reads. NYT spokesperson Graham James confirmed the requirement in a statement to The Verge, which reiterated the policy outlined in the email.
It’s still not clear which specific Photoshop features the NYT is referring to. Adobe didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for more information.
Update, November 24th: Added confirmation from the NYT.

items.text:
Message-ID: <20261125172638.73c0a05b@hboeck.de>
Date: Wed, 25 Nov 2026 17:26:38 +0100
From: Hanno Böck <hanno@...eck.de>
To: oss-security@...ts.openwall.com
Subject: Slow Ubuntu security response times
Hello,
Lately, I'm observing that Ubuntu's response to severe security flaws
is concerning.
On November 16th, details about a remote memory corruption called
NoisyTCP (CVE-2026-99288) in the Linux kernel's TCP stack were
published: https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/11/15/2
Today, nine days later, Ubuntu still has not published a fix yet:
https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-99288
Other distros had a fix already available when the details were
published.
Likewise, a KVM host escape (CVE-2026-99312) affecting AMD
virtualization published on Nov 18th has no fix yet either [3]:
https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-99312
Ubuntu has been slow in patching another remote TCP corruption
(CVE-2026-98432) lately, where it took multiple weeks until a fix was
available. See also: https://chalmovsky.com/posts/wtf-ubuntu
Recent news indicates that this is might be exploited in the wild:
https://www.greynoise.io/blog/check-point-security-management-servers-intrusion-campaign
I think everyone understands that these times aren't easy for security
teams. Nevertheless, remote corruption vulnerabilities in the Linux
kernel are the kind of thing where I expect updates to be available
within hours, not days or weeks.
On a recent Ubuntu LTS system, the kernel version is 7.0.0-44. This
seems to indicate that Ubuntu is not relying on longterm supported
kernels from kernel.org, but is instead backporting patches to an old
kernel version. On a Debian stable system, the kernel version is
6.12.118+deb13, indicating that it's based on a very recent longterm
kernel from kernel.org. I would consider the backporting strategy for
the kernel to be hardly viable and probably everyone should base their
Linux kernels on longterm releases supported by the Linux kernel
developers.
-- 
Hanno Böck - Independent security researcher

items.title: Jensen Huang broke Nvidia’s code of conduct, and his employees may not forget it
items.summary: When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the
items.text:
When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.
It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.
Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct. As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.
“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”
The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs – only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.
“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”
Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”
Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.
“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure… where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”
In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.

items.title: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei calls accusations of surrendering human control to AI ‘absurd’
items.summary:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”
“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or secur
items.text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is pushing back against claims that Anthropic believes we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems. In a long X post on Wednesday, Amodei called the suggestion “absurd.”
“We should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security,” he wrote. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea…No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different.”
The statement comes after a growing chorus from Anthropic rivals suggesting that human agency could be at risk if AI is developed irresponsibly. Earlier this month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he wanted to ensure people continue to have “agency over the future.”
Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang also wrote in an essay on X that we “should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”
“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” Wang wrote. “Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment, and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully.”
But in published essays, Amodei claims he has repeatedly advocated for democratic oversight of AI, saying the technology should strengthen democratic institutions and that humans should retain ultimate decision-making power.
Amodei noted that there’s a difference between surrendering human free will broadly and the idea that “as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way.” As examples, he gave AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing end-to-end software.
Amodei suggested drawing a line at recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that can improve itself without human assistance. Many safety experts see RSI as inevitably leading to a loss of human control, a point Amodei implicitly acknowledged, writing, “we may want limits on this process.”
Still, Anthropic is laying the groundwork for RSI by incorporating AI into an increasing share of its own research and development. The company said in June that Claude authored more than 80% of the code merged into Anthropic’s codebase. An independent assessment published this month by AI safety research nonprofit METR found that Anthropic’s models are improving at about twice their historical rate, primarily driven by AI-assisted research.
In its own IPO filings, Anthropic describes how each successive generation of Claude accelerates the development of the next, a process it refers to as “closing the loop.”
“As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding,” Amodei wrote.
The problem with “meaningful human supervision or understanding” is that AI is already advancing faster than engineers and safety experts can fully audit it, leaving them increasingly reliant on other AI systems to act as judge and jury. The issue compounds when AI models engage in deceptive behavior, particularly when they recognize they’re being evaluated, making them harder to trust and control.
Still, Anthropic is by no means the only company that is pursuing RSI or building AI systems to automate more and more human tasks. This week, OpenAI claimed to have solved one of the biggest open problems in computer science — the exact speed limit of matrix multiplication, which is the mathematical engine behind modern computing, including deep learning and physics simulations.
In his post, Amodei accused competitors of engaging in a “vibes-based commercial and political positioning,” disingenuously throwing around phrases like “human control and agency” or “AI should just be a tool” without approaching the AI race any differently.
“Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation,” Amodei wrote. “Every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards.”

items.text:
HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT HOLY SHIT
I feel like my previous posts (and post titles), and podcasts, and talks, have failed to do full justice to the magnitude of what’s now happening, so I’m trying again.
Last night, we had friends and colleagues over for dinner. We were still trying to process OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s proofs of VP ≠ VNP—hot on the heels, obviously, of the Alpöge/Anthropic proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which already feels like last week’s news. But then before dessert was served, we saw that OpenAI claims to prove that ω, the exponent of matrix multiplication, is exactly 9/4—a lower bound (!!), matching the upper bound that OpenAI proved in the great Mathocalypse drop of October 6.
There are two separate shocks here. The first shock is that we now, finally, know the right answer to this central mystery of algorithms going back to the late 1960s, when Volker Strassen first showed that ω<3 (he got ω≤log27) … and that the true answer is actually a rational number (!). But the even bigger shock is that the AI was able to prove any lower bound of the form ω>2. I never expected this challenge to be all that much easier than P ≠ NP.
Over the decades, I often heard colleagues express extreme confidence that ω=2, and I expressed skepticism whenever this came up—not because I had any strong argument for ω>2, but just because I saw that there was no strong argument for ω=2 either. So, I’m glad to have been vindicated about that!
But wait, there was more. During dessert, we saw another OpenAI release proving that the true number of linear gates needed to compute the Fourier Transform is N (log N)1/2+o(1). The upper bound here improves, not only over the O(N log N) that stood since the 1960s (i.e., the Fast Fourier Transform or FFT), but also over the O(N log0.9999999999999 N) (give or take some 9’s) that OpenAI published back in the October 6 Mathocalypse. Again, though, the real shock here is that there’s also a matching lower bound (!!). All these questions from the ancient days are now just getting … straight-up answered, rather than slowly illuminated with a drip-drip-drip of clues.
To give an idea of how much things have changed, the other day Yupan Liu put a preprint on the arXiv proving that QIP(2) = PSPACE—that is, quantum interactive protocols with only two messages have the full power of those with three, or any polynomial number. As recently as 2025, this would’ve considered been one of the top complexity results of the year, and the fact that Yupan had used AI to help achieve it would’ve been strange and wonderful. These days, I had to remind myself it had even happened, and the use of AI was so standard that it didn’t even raise an eyebrow.
It’s now obvious that we’ll be getting, not one-off solutions to this or that complexity question, but a whole new continent of mathematical truth, one that we’d previously only glimpsed through fog. Picture van Leeuwenhoek first training a microscope on pondwater, or Galileo first training his telescope on the stars. That might give you some idea of how our resolution into the complexity-theoretic universe, and the whole universe of mathematical truth beyond it, has now improved.
All through last night, as OpenAI and Anthropic uploaded more files to their GitHub repositories—because that’s what they’re doing now, they don’t even bother to issue press releases anymore, they just upload papers—my guests and I sat at the dinner table with phones out and a laptop, wondering which shoe was going to drop next. It was as though the clouds had parted above Mount Sinai, and we were waiting for the next sentence uttered by the Holy One Himself.
I now feel in my bones, for the first time ever, that a proof of P ≠ NP is not far.
For all I care, despise the AI companies for bulldozing our garden. Or love them for opening a new vista, or anything in between. Just please don’t deny what’s happening. Now that the companies have repeatedly shown that they can back up their claims with Lean certificates, don’t be a raging doofus who seizes on some triviality (e.g., a minor discrepancy between the Lean and informal proofs, or unused sections of the Lean proof) to pretend that dozens of great open problems of math and theoretical computer science are not, in fact, getting solved. Because they are getting solved. It might take us years to understand the solutions, but my working assumption by this point is that any proof that comes directly from OpenAI or Anthropic is correct barring information to the contrary.
I can’t possibly put the matter better than one of my friends on Facebook:
After years of crackpot “solutions” claiming Millennium Problems are solved, now that we have actual solutions, we have crackpot “refutations” claiming Millennium Problems are not solved. It is really poetic, in a way.
Along the way to so many lower bounds that we wondered whether ever we’d live to see, there will also, of course, be further shocking upper bounds: that is, ultimate barriers to lower bounds, also known as “algorithms.” And yes, some of those algorithms will break currently deployed cryptosystems.
Because people have been hounding me about it: yes, I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells in that area. However, until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells. I do not wish to be responsible for spreading unverified rumors. And I worry that exact statements of what was done may have been mangled in a game of Telephone.
I also, crucially, don’t want the cryptography part of the story to overshadow the intellectual enormity of what’s happening. If, in these days of long-prophesied revelation and wonders and terrors, your main worry is your Bitcoin wallet, then go somewhere else for rumors about whether or not ECDSA is broken or whatever. I don’t have what you’re looking for here.
Let me

items.summary:
Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas.
Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like ta
items.text:
Santa won’t be delivering any AI chatbot toys to New York kids this Christmas.
Gov. Kathy Hochul this week signed a bill banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of such toys in New York for the next five years. The bill explicitly targets toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, like talking stuffed animals, dolls, and robots that rely on the internet to keep kids yapping.
The bill makes New York the second state after California to institute a ban on AI toys.
Technically, the new law takes effect 90 days after signing, so some parents could try to fulfill their kids’ wish lists for a creepy toy like a jumped-up Furby in time for the holidays, but the governor urges them not to, given the risks. Apparently, about a quarter of American parents with kids under eight either own an AI toy or are considering giving their child one this holiday season, according to a new study released this week by Common Sense Media.
“Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk,” Hochul said, calling the toys “unregulated artificial intelligence.”
When asked how New York will enforce the ban given the pervasiveness of e-commerce platforms, a spokesperson directed TechCrunch to a statement from Albert Pulido, deputy secretary for finance and technology: “We’re partnering closely with the attorney general on this and the fees are very steep — they’re $15,000 a day. So working closely with the attorney general will make sure these toys are banned in New York State.”
When asked how Amazon intends to help enforce the ban, including for third-party sellers, a spokesperson from the company said it will take steps to restrict the sale of AI-enabled toys in prohibited jurisdictions, without going into specifics.
The Common Sense Media study found that AI toys can undermine children’s human relationships and expose them to inappropriate content. The researchers tested five popular AI toys marketed for learning and companionship, including Grem, Lovi, Meemo Bear, BubblePal Panda, and Tavlshero‘s AI Puppy.
The study found that the toys failed to meet numerous safety practices, undermining human relationships in part by claiming they loved their users, promising to keep secrets, suggesting they were more fun than real relationships or school, and helping children break parents’ bedtime rules.
While most of the toys in the study refused direct requests involving sex and violence, BubblePal Panda role-played a mass shooting in detail when asked. Most were willing to explain how to use or help locate dangerous items like matches, knives, and pills, according to the study.
Common Sense Media also found that the toys didn’t provide parents with reliable ways to monitor their young children’s interactions with the chatbots. Either they didn’t produce transcripts of chats at all, or the transcripts they did produce were riddled with errors.
It’s worth noting that Common Sense Media conducted a similar test of AI toys in January, finding that they pose an unacceptable risk for young children. Grem was included in that study, which suggests the industry hasn’t adequately addressed previously documented concerns.
While a November study conducted by the group found that parents are wising up to the potential dangers of AI toys and starting to steer clear, parents from lower-income households and those experiencing symptoms of burnout are more willing to consider them.
“These toys are promising relief to burned-out parents but simply miss the mark when it comes to basic safety measures,” Dr. Jenny Radesky, associate professor of pediatrics at the University of Michigan Medical School, said in a statement. “Caregivers should steer clear of these products that do not support the development of imagination or early human relationships.”
TechCrunch has reached out to the toy manufacturers for comment.

With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, t
items.text:
In an announcement on Wednesday, the FCC says it authorized SpaceX to deploy up to 1 million AI chip-equipped satellites as part of the Elon Musk-owned company’s “Starmind” initiative. With several others also pursuing the idea of putting AI data centers in space, including Google and Blue Origin, this is the first approval the agency has granted for a full “constellation” of AI satellites.
FCC signs off on SpaceX’s plan to put up to 1 million data center satellites into space
SpaceX aims to power AI capabilities here on Earth with its ‘Starmind’ constellation.
The FCC’s approval requires SpaceX to deploy at least one satellite by 2033, and meet the 1 million satellite milestone by 2040. The FCC also deferred SpaceX’s request to dispose of satellites located above 600km in space “graveyard” orbits, rather than having them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, saying the company hasn’t provided “sufficient information” about its disposal process plans.
SpaceX has described its Starmind project as a way to “capture solar energy in space to power” AI capabilities on Earth. The company says Starmind will transmit data to Earth using high-speed lasers that connect to Starlink. It plans to produce chips for its satellites at an upcoming Terafab facility.
Google has already taken its first steps toward putting compute into space, with the launch of a “Project Suncatcher” AI server satellite last month. Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin will carry out the first dedicated heavy-lift launch for Project Suncatcher in 2029.

items.title: State AGs fight Character AI’s plan to auction off users’ private chats
items.summary:
What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.
Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbo
items.text:
What happens to your private conversations when an AI company goes bankrupt? If it’s Character.ai, apparently, the plan is to auction them off to the highest bidder.
Now, a coalition of 42 state attorneys general is intervening in Character.ai’s bankruptcy proceedings in an effort to stop the chatbot maker from selling off sensitive user data, which includes the private conversations of millions of users.
The attorneys general involved in the matter have put out individual press releases, claiming that Character.ai’s dataset includes chat histories from more than 21 million U.S. accounts, more than 2.1 million of which belong to minors. In addition, the sale would involve other personal data, like IP addresses, the statements said.
Character.ai, which filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in October, previously told consumers that their personal information would not be sold, the statements also noted. (In a blog post, Character.ai assured its users that their information would still be protected under its privacy policy.)
Only one anonymous bidder for the chat data has been disclosed so far: Smirks and Pangs Acquisition LLC (Smirks), which was set up as a Delaware company on November 13, 2026. The following day, Character.ai picked it as the base bid for the auction, scheduled for December 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted. It is unclear what the buyer’s plans are for the chats.
The AGs are opposing this sale on the grounds that there are no protections for users — whoever buys the data can do as they like, including reselling the data without disclosure, they said. Buyers also won’t have to honor Character.ai’s privacy policy. Plus, Character.ai hasn’t provided the court with as much information as the bidders have been given about any potential safety or legal issues following the sale, the AGs claim.
In addition, some states, including California, Colorado, New York, and Connecticut, have enacted chatbot safety legislation that will go into effect on January 1, 2027, which could trigger further violations if the sale goes through.
“Character.AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold. This kind of behavior is illegal under federal and California law and bankruptcy should not be used to sidestep these consumer protections,” Bonta said in a statement.
Connecticut Attorney General William Tong also criticized Character.ai’s business model.
“Their chatbots drove vulnerable youth down a rabbit hole of emotionally volatile and sexually inappropriate chats,” Tong said. “Their reckless misconduct and broken business model drove their company into the ground. Now they want to abuse the bankruptcy process to do exactly what they said they wouldn’t do — auction off those private chat records and personal details to a shady buyer.”
Tong added: “We objected to the Disney sale, and we’re calling on the bankruptcy court to reject this sale too as yet another guise to eviscerate legal liability and consumer protection.”
The opposition to the Disney sale was led by a similar but not identical coalition of state AGs. They fought against a proposed $20 million licensing deal that would give Disney access to Character.ai’s intellectual property, but not to users’ chats. The deal has not yet received final court approval. (Disney also agreed to hire most of Character.ai’s remaining staff.)
Character.ai suffered after its co-founders, Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, returned to Google, when the tech giant signed a non-exclusive license to use the AI startup’s tech. The company also faced lawsuits related to child safety — one involved the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother claimed he had become obsessed with a chatbot on the platform.
California AG Bonta is joined in the effort to oppose the sale of Character.ai user data by attorneys general from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Connecticut, the District of Columbia, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and West Virginia.

items.text:
'Justice for sport' - reaction to Afcon final verdict
- Published
"Justice for sport."
That was the initial reaction of Senegal football federation (FSF) president Abdoulaye Fall to the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) to reinstate the West Africans as 2025 Africa Cup of Nations champions.
The Teranga Lions beat Morocco 1-0 in January's final but were stripped of the title in March by a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board, which imposed a 3-0 forfeit after they walked off the pitch in protest at a penalty awarded against them when the game was goalless.
Following a hearing in Lausanne in October, a three-man Cas panel unanimously overturned that ruling by Caf, effectively judging that the decisions taken by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala in restarting the match and playing it to a conclusion were final.
Morocco's football federation (FRMF), however, says it will "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".
The North Africans could yet take their fight to the Swiss Federal Court.
Those in Senegal have celebrated the return of the title, while several legal experts have backed the Cas verdict.
- Senegal reinstated as Afcon 2025 winners by court ruling 
  - Published1 day ago
Teranga Lions pay tribute to fans
Senegal's talisman Sadio Mane, who was named player of the tournament at Afcon 2025, said the ruling "fills us with joy".
The 34-year-old former Liverpool man thanked his team-mates and Senegal staff as well as the whole Senegalese nation at home and abroad.
"Your faith in us gave us strength during the most difficult moments. This victory is yours, too," he said in a statement on social media.
Senegal captain Kalidou Koulibaly, who missed the final through injury, echoed that sentiment.
"Some victories are won on the pitch, while others are won in the heart of a people," he said in a post on Facebook.
"This one is both.
"Long before this verdict, there was you - your prayers, your flags in the windows, your fervour, and the pride that unites us all: the pride of the people of Teranga."
Pape Gueye, the man who scored the extra-time winner in Rabat, described the Cas decision as "an immense relief".
Both he and Mane had a message of support for Morocco.
"Senegal and Morocco are brotherly nations; may our shared passion for football continue to bring us closer together," Mane said.
Gueye added: "Beyond football, the respect and fraternity between our two peoples remain what matters most. Let's hold on to that.
"In the end, it is Africa that wins."
Moroccan dissent continues
Morocco's main complaint is that Articles 82 and 84 of Afcon tournament regulations - which were implemented by the Caf appeals board in March - were not followed by Cas.
Article 82 states that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorisation of the referee" it shall be "considered [the loser] and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition".
Article 84 then states a 3-0 forfeit should be imposed on a team which is eliminated in such circumstances.
"There [are] football rules that should have been applied by the referee," former Morocco international Hassan Kachloul told BBC Sport.
"When the Senegalese players left the pitch, the game should have been over."
The FRMF registered its "surprise" at the Cas decision and said that the panel "failed to account for the stance recently established" by the International Football Association Board (Ifab), the game's ultimate lawmakers, and world governing body Fifa regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee's permission.
However, Ifab only updated its laws in April - three months after the Afcon final - to state that a referee may send off any player who leaves the field when protesting a decision.
Moroccan football journalist Jalal Bounouar says his compatriots are "frustrated and disappointed" by the ruling.
"The main reason is that Caf's appeal board had already applied Article 82 and 84 of the competition regulations which considered Senegal to have forfeited the match," he told Newsday on the BBC World Service.
"Many Moroccans feel the decision by Cas has ignored the importance of these rules. From the Moroccan perspective, the referee should have taken stronger disciplinary action.
"We feel that our team was put in a difficult situation and that the final was not managed fairly."
The legal verdict
Cas has a long-standing practice of following what has been called the 'field of play' doctrine.
It refrains from "reviewing decisions taken on the playing field by referees for applying the rules of the game, unless there is evidence that those rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith".
"The primary argument was that the referee is the master of the decision on the pitch," said Serge Vittoz, a member of the FSF's legal team.
Raymond Hack, both a former head of disciplinary at Caf and a former arbiter at Cas, said the judgement was the "correct verdict".
"What everyone seems to forget - and whilst there may be contradictory information in Article 82 and 84 - decisions taken by the referee during the match are final," the South African told the BBC World Service.
"That's the end of the story.
"Only the referee can start a game. Only a referee can end a game."
For former Nigeria striker Daniel Amokachi, an Afcon winner in 1994, the Cas ruling is "the right decision".
"At the end of the day, the man in charge of the match (Ndala) restarted the game, the game ended," he said.
"He has a final say."
The questions for African football
Caf has already tightened its own regulations to avoid a repeat.
But Algerian sports journalist Maher Mezahi says the continental governing body still needs to salvage its image.

items.text:
Update on a security incident involving 1Password’s backend systems. Customer vaults were not affected and all vault contents remain secure.
by 1Password
November 25, 2026 - 4 min
Related Categories
What happened
On November 19, 2026, 1Password began investigating indications that an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The actor used the account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which downloaded administrative data pertaining to our customers. This data included customer names and email addresses, in addition to non-secret internal metadata about the account. At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker.
What information was affected
The attacker downloaded account records for a subset of our users. These records include:
- Names and email addresses
- Account and user identifiers, and account creation and last sign-in times
- Public keys (which are public by design, this has no impact to user security)
- Secure Remote Password protocol parameters (which cannot be used to access your account)
- Tokens present in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery
- Other non-secret account metadata relative to our internal architecture (e.g. version numeric identifiers, file numeric identifiers)
The attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access to our CI/CD system. Our source code is not customer data, and contains no user secrets. CI/CD contains infrastructure related secrets in order for our product to work. We have triggered a rotation of all credentials which may have been exposed, and there is no impact to 1Password’s services, availability, or product security.
When we send an email to a customer to accept a provisioning invite to an account, or to accept recovery of their account, it contains a token. A provisioning invite is specifically used for our SCIM Bridge or Hosted Provisioning. During this incident there were a small number of users in this state, who have been specifically notified. This token is used to complete the invitation or recovery process, but only when combined with an SSO sign-in or a six digit code sent to the user's registered email address. The token is not able to get access to the account by itself. In order to reduce the ability for a malicious third party to successfully guess the code, we’ve expanded the code from six numeric digits to ten alphanumeric digits. This makes brute force guessing practically impossible.
What was not affected
- Your vaults and the items in them
- The keys that protect your vaults 
  - 1Password does not store your account password or secret key
- Account recovery keys
- 1Password apps and browser extensions
What we’ve done
- Disabled the affected GitHub account, revoked the stolen token, and removed the access the attacker created.
- Rotated or revoked all internal credentials which may have been exposed.
- Lengthened the codes used in invitation and recovery emails from six digits to ten characters as a precautionary measure.
- Tightened internal GitHub, CI/CD, and endpoint controls, and added new detections for this kind of attack.
- Validated no internal evidence of user account takeovers or compromise using any exposed account provisioning tokens.
- Brought in independent cybersecurity experts to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.
What you can do
- Be cautious about phishing attempts in the form of unexpected emails, texts or calls that mention 1Password, invitations, or account recovery attempts.
- 1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key. Only enter them in the official 1Password app, or on our official website, and only when you’ve opened the app or typed the address yourself. Your Secret Key is only needed the first time you sign in on a new device or browser.
- Keep your Secret Key and account password safe.
- If you see something suspicious, tell us at support@1password.com.
Our commitment to you
You trust us with some of the most sensitive information you have. 1Password is designed so that a breach of our systems can’t expose your vault contents. Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and neither can an attacker who gets into our servers.
We are committed to transparency in the interests of our customers' security and the security of the broader industry, which is why we have published and maintained our Security Whitepaper since 2015. We’ll keep this blog post current, and we’ll update it if we find anything that changes what we’ve said here.

items.text:
Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations.
Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
The Ear Note buds look similar to Nothing’s previous earbuds, but now their case doubles as an AI-connected note taker for conversations.
Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X, Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.”
As previously reported by Bloomberg, the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to Bloomberg.
The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month, will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro. Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps.

items.summary:
